title: Start here · a sequence you can follow
text:
This course follows  Corner Market , a fictional neighborhood marketplace. Begin with one request and one database. Add a distributed component only after identifying the failure or capacity limit it addresses. All traffic figures are teaching assumptions, not facts about any company. 
 Start here: three paths through one sequence    Path  Sequence and proof of learning    New to design · 8 weeks  Weeks 1–2: requirements, estimates, APIs, concurrency and storage. Weeks 3–4: caching through messaging. Week 5: reliability and multi-region. Weeks 6–8: two cases per week, then a timed redesign. Spend 5–7 hours per week; repeat a week when the exit task fails.    Experienced builder · 4 weeks  Run the labs and explain every failed invariant first. Study the missed foundations. Solve URL shortener, reservations and streaming; then choose two unfamiliar cases. Write an operational rollback plan for each.    Principal preparation · 2 week diagnostic sprint  Review constraints, correctness, reliability and evolution. Solve three unseen cases with a partner. Require explicit ownership, migration, cost model and failure containment. This is a diagnostic, not a shortcut to principal experience.   
 Prerequisites and exit criteria  You should be able to read a Python function, explain a dictionary lookup, write a SQL SELECT, and distinguish a byte from a bit. A byte is eight bits; 1 MB here means 1,000,000 bytes, so a 10 MB/s payload is 80 Mb/s before protocol overhead. A SQL query such as  SELECT n FROM stock WHERE id=1  reads the column n from the matching row. A Python dictionary maps keys to values; its lookup is expected constant time under ordinary hash assumptions. If Python functions or basic SQL are new, learn those prerequisites first; the labs below are application exercises rather than a complete programming introduction. Run  python3 labs/design.py  and manually trace its assertions once those basics are comfortable. No cloud account or package installation is needed.   High-level design (HLD)  assigns responsibilities to services and stores and explains data movement, capacity and failure behavior.  Low-level design (LLD)  specifies interfaces, state transitions and concurrency within a component. A box marked “payment service” is HLD; the permitted transition from pending to captured and its idempotency key are LLD. A convincing answer connects both. 
 A 45 minute interview method    0–5 minutes:  restate the user action, define scope, ask for peak load, durability and freshness. Name one invariant: a condition that must always hold.   5–10:  estimate requests per second, bytes per day and concurrent work. Keep units. Decide which number actually changes the design.   10–15:  define two APIs, the source of truth and keys. Trace a successful write and read.   15–25:  draw a minimal working system. Label synchronous calls, durable writes and asynchronous edges. Explain the acknowledgment boundary.   25–35:  choose two deep dives driven by the prompt. Trace a retry after an ambiguous timeout and a dependency failure.   35–42:  evaluate skew, recovery, privacy, cost and growth. Explain one rejected alternative.   42–45:  summarize assumptions, the largest remaining risk and the experiment that would validate it.   If the interviewer changes the scale, revise the bottleneck and retain unaffected decisions. Do not restart by naming fashionable components. Ask permission to spend time on correctness when the prompt involves money or inventory. 
 How to use each lesson  Read the request trace, then cover the solution and reproduce it. Change one assumption: tenfold load, a slow replica, a duplicate message, or a regional partition. Explain which guarantee changes and why. Answer disclosures remain closed until you open them. Diagrams are plain text with labeled edges so they remain selectable, zoomable and usable without a graphics library.   First diagnostic: the checkout timed out. Should the client retry?  The timeout does not prove failure. The server may have committed the order before its response was lost. Retry the same logical operation with a stable idempotency key and query its durable result. A new key can create a second order. A blanket “never retry writes” also fails availability goals.  
 Evidence of mastery  The study checkbox records reading in your browser only. It is not a score. Keep a separate notebook with: the original invariant, a diagram, unit-bearing estimates, a failure trace, the selected tradeoff and a retrospective after feedback. Re-solve after 48 hours without notes. A correct answer you cannot defend under changed assumptions is recognition, not mastery.  There are no analytics, paid API calls, external scripts or interview guarantees. Technical references are linked in context and reviewed on 19 October 2026. Product behavior can change; verify vendor documentation before implementing a real service.

title: 1. Turn an ambiguous prompt into a contract
text:
Start with a person and a decision 
 Corner Market is a fictional service connecting residents with local grocers. A shopper browses produce, reserves stock, pays, and collects an order. The examples are teaching assumptions, never claims about a real business. A system is the cooperating software, data, people, and operating procedures that deliver that journey. System design means choosing their boundaries and behavior under constraints. Before drawing boxes, say what success means for a shopper and what must never happen. 
 A functional requirement describes behavior: reserve three apples for ten minutes. A nonfunctional requirement describes a quality of that behavior: finish most reservations quickly despite a failed server. An invariant is a rule that every valid state preserves: available stock never becomes negative. Availability is whether a request receives a useful response; durability is whether acknowledged data survives failures. These words answer different questions. A fast error is available only if the contract counts that error as useful. 
 Clarify the contract 
 Ask who uses the system, the three essential journeys, scope exclusions, traffic shape, data retention, geographic footprint, acceptable staleness, and failure expectations. Offer concrete choices. “Can a catalog show yesterday's price?” is better than “Do we need consistency?” Assume one city initially, catalog prices stale for at most sixty seconds, stock checked when reserving, and payment settlement handled by an external provider. Exclude delivery routing and tax calculation from the first interview. Record these assumptions visibly so an interviewer can change them. 
 Separate a business promise from an implementation guess. “One successful payment capture per order” is a promise. “Use a distributed lock” is a candidate mechanism whose failure behavior needs proof. Ask what happens when a customer presses Pay twice, loses connectivity, or returns after a reservation expires. Those scenarios expose requirements that a component list misses. Include an explicit owner for every authoritative fact: inventory owns quantity; orders own checkout state; the payment provider reports money movement. 
 Before distributing: one machine can already race  A process is a running program with its own memory space. Threads share a process's memory; separate processes generally do not share ordinary Python objects. An event loop runs tasks cooperatively: an awaiting task yields so another can run. Concurrency means operations overlap in time; parallelism means operations execute simultaneously. Two tasks can race even on one thread if a read and later write are separated by an await. Two servers each have their own local lock, so neither lock protects the other server's stock update.  Trace one request: accept a socket, authenticate, acquire a bounded database connection, begin a transaction, conditionally change stock, commit, release the connection, respond. A connection pool reuses a limited set of database connections; it is not extra database capacity. If every request opens a new connection during a burst, setup and connection limits can fail before useful work starts. Bound waiting, keep transactions short, and let the database protect shared stock. The invariant stays the same when the application grows from one process to many.  A forty-five-minute interview 
 Spend minutes zero through five defining journeys and invariants; five through ten estimating the dominant load; ten through twenty choosing APIs, records, and the simplest end-to-end design; twenty through thirty-five exploring the two highest-risk decisions; thirty-five through forty-two analyzing failures and evolution; and the final three minutes summarizing choices and unresolved risks. This is a negotiation aid, not a rigid performance script. Ask whether the interviewer prefers correctness, scale, or operations before selecting deep dives. 
  HLD  explains why an order service talks to inventory and how failures cross that boundary.  LLD  explains the reservation state machine, repository interface, and concurrency-safe update. Move between levels when it resolves a risk. Writing twenty classes before deciding whether stock may oversell is premature; drawing services without explaining one atomic stock update is incomplete. 
 Build and challenge the smallest design 
 Begin with a web application and relational database. Follow one reserve request from authentication through validation, conditional inventory update, order creation, commit, and response. Then deliberately break a dependency: the response is lost after commit. The client cannot distinguish this from a failed commit, so introduce a stable request identifier and a retrievable result. Add a queue only when email should succeed independently from checkout; add a cache only when a measured read bottleneck or geographic latency calls for one. 
 A useful drawing labels arrows with operation and protocol, stores with ownership, and boundaries with failure scope. Write the invariant beside the transaction boundary. Every new component should answer three questions: what pressure requires it, what new failure does it create, and how will operators know that it works? A principal-level discussion also identifies the team that can operate the choice and a migration plan that avoids rewriting everything simultaneously. 
  Practice: the interviewer says “design a grocery app.” What do you say first?  “I will focus on browsing, reserving inventory, and checkout. Is one city sufficient? Must we prevent overselling, and can catalog data lag by sixty seconds? I assume one successful capture per order and external payment processing. I will first show a working single-region flow, then explore hot inventory and payment timeouts.” This makes scope and correctness reviewable. A weak answer immediately names five databases without establishing any promise.  
 Completion check: write a one-page contract for a library hold system using the same method, then explain which grocery assumptions no longer apply. Reading this chapter is study completion; doing that exercise with a changed prompt supplies evidence of transfer.

title: 2. Estimate load with units and uncertainty
text:
Estimate to change a decision 
 Capacity estimation is a simplified model of resources needed to serve a workload. It is useful when it chooses between designs or reveals an impossible promise. Corner Market has 100,000 daily active shoppers, each opening twenty catalog pages and placing 0.2 orders per day. These are explicit fictional baseline assumptions used throughout this foundation sequence. A day contains 86,400 seconds. Assume a tenfold peak-to-average factor for requests, a 2 KB decimal catalog response excluding photos, a 1 KB order record before indexes, and thirty-day hot order retention. 
 Catalog traffic is 100,000 × 20 = 2,000,000 requests/day. Dividing by 86,400 gives approximately 23.15 requests/second on average and 231.5 at the assumed peak. Orders are 100,000 × 0.2 = 20,000/day, approximately 0.2315/second average and 2.315/second peak. Do not say “millions of users require sharding”: this baseline may fit a modest database. Search, photos, expensive joins, geographic distance, and bursts may matter more than total user count. 
 Keep units attached 
 Two million catalog responses × 2,000 bytes equals 4,000,000,000 bytes/day, or 4 GB using decimal units. Peak response bandwidth is 231.5 × 2,000 = 463,000 bytes/second, approximately 3.704 megabits/second before headers, encryption, retries, and images. Eight bits make one byte. A gigabyte is 10^9 bytes; a gibibyte is 2^30 bytes. State which convention you use, especially when comparing storage bills and memory capacity. 
 Orders consume 20,000 × 1,000 = 20 MB/day of raw rows, or 600 MB in thirty days. If an illustrative combined allowance for row overhead and indexes doubles raw storage, the working primary needs 1.2 GB. Three full database copies require 3.6 GB for those rows and indexes, excluding write logs, backups, free space, and unrelated tables. Replication is a copy multiplier, not a substitute for estimating backup history. A deletion policy changes both cost and recovery requirements. 
 Concurrency and service time 
 Concurrency is work in progress. For a stable system, average work in progress equals arrival rate times average time in the system; this is Little's Law. At 231.5 requests/second and 0.2 seconds average response time, approximately 46.3 requests are in flight. This does not mean forty-seven CPU cores are required: much of the time may be waiting for a database or network. If each request actually consumes 5 milliseconds of CPU time, that workload consumes 1.1575 CPU-seconds per second before overhead, suggesting more than one fully utilized core and headroom for bursts. 
 Utilization is the fraction of resource capacity in use. Queueing delays rise sharply as arrivals approach service capacity, so a benchmark at maximum throughput is not a safe operating target. Measure throughput together with tail latency: p99 is the response time below which ninety-nine percent of observations fall. Percentiles do not add across services. A whole-request p99 cannot be obtained by simply adding each dependency's p99 because their slow events may overlap or occur on different requests. 
 Model the awkward workload 
 A flash sale can invalidate the tenfold assumption. Suppose 5,000 shoppers attempt to reserve the same item within one second. Total catalog load remains unremarkable, but one inventory row receives 5,000 contending writes. A hot key is one identifier receiving disproportionate traffic. More database shards do not divide one indivisible stock counter. Consider admission control, a waiting room, partitioned stock allocations with reconciliation, or accepting fewer requests while preserving the invariant. Select the mechanism only after discussing acceptable customer behavior. 
 Use sensitivity analysis: recompute the result when an uncertain input changes. At 200 KB per page instead of 2 KB, catalog transfer becomes 400 GB/day. At a hundredfold peak rather than tenfold, peak request rate becomes 2,315/second. Write low, expected, and high assumptions; identify which measurement you would collect first. Load tests should reproduce skew, cold caches, slow dependencies, and retry storms, not just uniform random successful reads. 
  Practice: a worker drains 150 jobs/second while 250 arrive each second for two minutes. What backlog forms?  The deficit is 100 jobs/second, so 12,000 jobs accumulate after 120 seconds, assuming zero initial backlog and constant rates. When arrivals fall to 50/second, net drainage is 100/second, requiring another 120 seconds. “Autoscale workers” is incomplete unless the downstream database can absorb their added load.  
 Exit artifact: a worksheet with assumptions, equations, units, peak factors, uncertainty ranges, and the architectural decision each estimate informs. Recalculate without a calculator first, then verify arithmetic; order-of-magnitude mistakes should become visible before precision distracts you. 
 Request trace: Resource bounds  At a flash sale, 5,000 shoppers arrive; a bounded admission queue accepts a safe subset; the rest receive explicit retry guidance. If each rejected client retries immediately, offered traffic grows. Keep admitted work below sustainable service capacity and test the retry policy, rather than multiplying server counts from daily averages.

title: 3. Follow a request and design a durable API
text:
Trace the path 
 A network request crosses independently failing boundaries. The shopper's client resolves a hostname using the  DNS , establishes a transport connection, negotiates  TLS , and sends an  HTTP  request. A load balancer distributes requests among healthy application instances. Connection reuse avoids repeating setup for every request, but a broken reused connection still needs bounded recovery. A server marked healthy may have a failing database, so distinguish process liveness from readiness to accept useful traffic. 
 Latency is elapsed time for one operation; throughput is completed operations per unit time. Greater bandwidth does not remove a long round trip. Four sequential dependent calls across a 70-millisecond path spend at least 280 milliseconds on those trips before processing. Batch independent lookups, colocate related operations, or redesign a chatty interface. Parallel calls help independent work but create additional load and complicate cancellation when the parent request no longer needs results. 
 A reservation contract 
 Expose  POST /v1/reservations  with a client-generated  Idempotency-Key , authenticated shopper identity, store identifier, item identifier, quantity, and expected price version. An idempotent effect means repeating an operation does not multiply its intended state change. This endpoint implements that property through a stored key scoped to the shopper and operation; merely naming a header does not provide it. Save a hash of the request body so reuse with different content is rejected. 
  POST /v1/reservations
Idempotency-Key: 7f2-example
{"store_id":"s7","item_id":"apple","quantity":3,"price_version":12}

201 Created
{"reservation_id":"r81","state":"held","expires_at":"...","version":1}  
 The schema is deliberately small. Quantity must be a positive bounded integer. Price is checked against a server-owned version. The response contains a stable identifier that  GET /v1/reservations/r81  can retrieve after a timeout. The key table stores shopper, operation, key, body hash, result identifier, and expiration. Commit the key and reservation together. Retain keys for the documented retry window; clients cannot assume protection after keys expire. 
 Errors are part of the interface 
 Return a structured error with a machine-readable code, human-readable message, request identifier, and retry guidance. Distinguish invalid quantity, unavailable stock, authorization failure, and temporary dependency failure. HTTP defines method and status semantics; for example, GET is safe, and PUT and DELETE have idempotent semantics, while POST is not inherently idempotent. Those properties concern intended server effects, not whether every repeated response has identical bytes. See  RFC 9110 , checked 2026-10-19. 
 A timeout tells the client it stopped waiting; it does not prove the server failed. Set a total request deadline and allocate smaller dependency timeouts within it. If a 500-millisecond server deadline allows a database call to wait two seconds, the work outlives its purpose. Propagate cancellation where supported, but preserve a committed operation's retrievable outcome. Retry only operations whose effects are safe to repeat, with a limited attempt count, increasing delay, and randomness to avoid synchronized retries. 
 Pagination, compatibility, and trust 
 For order history, sort by  (created_at, order_id)  and return an opaque cursor containing the last pair. Keyset pagination resumes from the last observed key; offset pagination skips a count of rows and can become expensive or unstable when new rows arrive. Define whether a browsing session sees a fixed snapshot or a changing history. Always add a unique tiebreaker because timestamps can coincide. 
 Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that identity may perform this operation on this object. Never accept a supplied shopper identifier as proof of ownership. Enforce authorization on each retrieved reservation and each mutation. Bound body sizes, item counts, and query complexity. Avoid putting secrets in URLs because URLs often enter logs. Version contracts by making additive changes first; removing a field requires evidence that old clients no longer depend on it. 
  Practice: POST times out, then the client retries with a new key. What breaks?  The server may interpret the retry as a second operation and hold stock twice. Retry with the same key and unchanged body, or retrieve the original result. If the original key is unknown because local client state was lost, show pending status and reconcile rather than claiming the first attempt failed.  
 Exit artifact: document one success, one business rejection, one authentication failure, and one uncertain outcome. Draw the entire request path and label every place a deadline, identity, or identifier must survive. 
 Predict an uncertain external outcome  Payment sequence: the client creates attempt P7; the service sends capture P7; the provider captures money; the response is lost; the local deadline expires. “Failed” is now an incorrect conclusion because the effect occurred. Store P7 as pending, retrieve provider status or retry under the provider's documented idempotency contract, then reconcile the order. The invariant is one successful capture per order. A local database rollback cannot roll back the provider.   Debug: would a longer timeout remove this failure mode?  No. It changes probability and waiting cost, but any finite deadline can expire after an effect occurs. Durable attempt identity and reconciliation address ambiguity.

title: 4. Model data around queries and invariants
text:
Choose the unit of truth 
 A data model defines records, relationships, valid states, and access patterns. Corner Market begins with stores, items, inventory, reservations, orders, and payment attempts. A primary key uniquely identifies a record; a foreign key constrains a reference to another record. Inventory belongs to a store-item pair. Reservations record quantity and expiration, while order lines preserve the purchased description and price. Copying the purchased price is intentional history: a later catalog edit must not rewrite an old receipt. 
  inventory(store_id, item_id, available, version)
  PRIMARY KEY(store_id, item_id), CHECK(available >= 0)
reservation(id, shopper_id, store_id, item_id, quantity, state, expires_at)
order_header(id, shopper_id, state, created_at)
order_line(order_id, item_id, quantity, unit_price_minor, currency)
request_key(shopper_id, operation, key, body_hash, result_id)
  UNIQUE(shopper_id, operation, key)  
 Money uses an integer in the currency's defined minor unit or a carefully selected decimal representation, with currency stored explicitly. Do not assume every currency has two decimal places. State transitions are explicit: held becomes confirmed or expired; confirmed does not silently become held again. A separate adjustment records a refund. The database is authoritative; a search index and cache are derived views that can be rebuilt. 
 Atomicity beats a hopeful read 
 A transaction groups operations that succeed or fail together. Atomicity means no partial committed result; isolation controls interference among concurrent transactions. For one stock row, use a conditional update and check the affected-row count, then insert the reservation in the same transaction: 
  BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 3, version = version + 1
WHERE store_id = 's7' AND item_id = 'apple' AND available >= 3;
-- continue only if exactly one row changed
INSERT INTO reservation (...) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;  
 Reading available stock into application memory, checking it, and later writing a new value can lose concurrent changes. The conditional update makes the eligibility check and decrement one database operation. A database constraint supplies a final guard. Multi-item orders need one transaction with consistent lock order, or an explicit partial-reservation workflow and compensation. A deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting on each other's locks; retry the aborted transaction with a bounded policy. 
 Isolation is a choice with consequences 
 Serializable isolation makes committed concurrent transactions behave like some serial ordering. It may abort work that must then be retried. PostgreSQL's default Read Committed isolation gives each statement its own committed snapshot; Repeatable Read provides a stable transaction snapshot but does not eliminate every serialization anomaly. Consult  PostgreSQL transaction isolation , checked 2026-10-19. These product-specific facts do not imply every database implements identically named levels the same way. 
 Consider an invariant across two rows: at least one on-call stock reconciliation worker must remain active. Two transactions can each observe two active workers and disable a different worker, leaving none. This is write skew: independent writes violate a shared predicate. Protect the actual invariant using a locked coordinating row, a serializable transaction with retries, or a model that makes the decision atomic. Choosing “a transaction” without identifying its isolation and locked data is insufficient. 
 Indexes buy reads with writes and space 
 An index is an auxiliary structure locating records without scanning every row. For  WHERE shopper_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 , consider an index on  (shopper_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) . Composite-index order should follow actual predicates and sort requirements. PostgreSQL documents how leading equality constraints affect multicolumn B-tree scans in  Multicolumn Indexes , checked 2026-10-19. Verify with realistic query plans and data distributions; adding every imaginable index increases write work and storage. 
 A relational store suits the first design because relationships and atomic updates dominate. Object storage suits large immutable product images; storing image bytes in order rows bloats transactional reads and backups. A document store may suit independently retrieved product documents, but denormalizing inventory into every document creates a synchronization problem. Choose based on operations and invariants rather than declaring one category universally faster. 
  Practice: how does reservation expiry avoid returning stock twice?  Within a transaction, change held to expired only when its state is still held and the deadline has passed. Return quantity only if that transition changed a row. Repeated expiry attempts then do nothing. Confirm and expire must contend over the same reservation state so only one transition wins. Test a race between those operations.  
 Exit artifact: write three important queries, propose their indexes, and state which invariant each transaction protects. Explain recovery when the process crashes before commit and after commit but before responding. 
 Predict two interleavings   Lost update:  stock starts at five. A reads five; B reads five; A computes four and writes four; B computes four and writes four. Two reservations were accepted but only one unit was deducted. The invariant is that decrements equal accepted quantities. A conditional database decrement, not application read-modify-write, fixes this single-row race.   Write skew:  workers A and B are both active. Transaction T1 reads both and sees two; T2 reads both and sees two; T1 disables A; T2 disables B; both commit under snapshot isolation without a shared write conflict. The invariant “at least one active worker” fails. Serialize the decision using one coordinating row or use serializable isolation with whole-transaction retries.   Transfer: does a mutex around one Python dictionary fix both database races?  Only for callers that actually share and obey that mutex in one process. Another process, script, or server bypasses it. Protect the invariant at the shared authoritative boundary and test concurrent database sessions.

title: 5. Cache with a freshness and failure contract
text:
A cache is a disposable copy 
 A cache stores data closer to its consumer or in a faster medium to reduce latency or repeated computation. It creates another version of reality. Corner Market can cache product descriptions because a short delay is tolerable; the final stock reservation still consults authoritative inventory. First define the maximum acceptable staleness, key ownership, invalidation mechanism, eviction behavior, and what happens when the cache disappears. A cache that is necessary to reconstruct purchases is functioning as a database and needs a different durability contract. 
 In cache-aside, the application checks a key, reads the database on a miss, and populates the cache. A hit returns the cached value. A  TTL  bounds an entry's residence time, not necessarily the age of the underlying fact if a stale source repopulates it. Use versioned product values and include the version in invalidation messages. Keep shopper-private results out of shared public keys; include tenant, authorization scope, language, and other response-shaping inputs where appropriate. 
 Calculate benefit and failure load 
 At the foundation baseline peak of 231.5 catalog requests/second, a ninety-percent hit ratio leaves approximately 23.15 database reads/second, assuming one database read per miss. If hits take 2 milliseconds and misses 20 milliseconds, the weighted mean lookup time is 0.9 × 2 + 0.1 × 20 = 3.8 milliseconds. That arithmetic does not predict p99 latency, because ten percent of requests still follow the slow path. Network time and application work are excluded from this illustrative calculation. 
 On complete cache failure, database load returns to 231.5 reads/second, ten times the warmed miss load. Provision that fallback capacity or deliberately shed some traffic. A cache miss storm occurs when many callers simultaneously refill the same missing data. Coalesce concurrent misses so one caller fetches while others await the same result. Add small random variation to expiration times to avoid synchronized expiry of an entire catalog. Bound refill concurrency so database survival takes priority over hit-ratio recovery. 
 Invalidate without hand-waving 
 Suppose reader A misses, reads old price version twelve, and pauses. Writer B commits version thirteen and deletes the cache key. Reader A then fills version twelve after the delete. “Delete on every write” did not prevent stale resurrection. A short TTL bounds this particular stale fill, but strict freshness needs a stronger mechanism: compare versions against a retained current-version marker when populating (not merely against the cached value, which may be absent). Keep a version tombstone beyond the maximum stale-reader lifetime, and atomically reject any refill older than that marker; otherwise eviction or deletion can erase the fence and permit stale resurrection. If that lifetime cannot be bounded, validate against the authority rather than claiming a strict freshness guarantee. Other options include using versioned immutable keys with an authoritative current-version pointer, or bypass the cache for the critical operation. Each mechanism has a coordination cost. 
 Write-through updates the backing store through a controlled path that also updates the cache. Write-behind acknowledges a cache update before later persistence and risks loss or reordering unless backed by durable machinery. Name the actual acknowledgment boundary; the label alone proves nothing. An event-driven invalidation channel may lag or lose an invalidation, so combine it with bounded expiration and monitoring when the freshness contract allows that compromise. Redis describes server-assisted client cache invalidation in its  client-side caching documentation , checked 2026-10-19; that mechanism still needs application failure handling. 
 Choose what to cache 
 Cache immutable image variants at a content delivery network, which serves bytes near clients. Use a filename derived from content or version so updated images have a new address. Cache catalog fragments with explicit freshness. Avoid shared caching of payment status unless the key and response policy preserve authorization and the product accepts delay. Negative caching stores a not-found result briefly; it reduces repeated misses but can hide a newly created object until expiry. Limit its duration and distinguish a genuine absence from a temporary database failure. 
 A cache eviction policy chooses entries to discard under pressure. Least recently used approximates the belief that recently accessed objects are likely to be accessed again. A scan through millions of cold items can still evict valuable entries. Observe hit ratio by endpoint, object size, refill latency, eviction rate, and source load. A ninety-nine-percent global hit ratio can conceal a business-critical endpoint with no useful hits. 
  Practice: should checkout trust a cached price that is forty seconds old?  Only if the business contract explicitly promises that price or accepts that age. A safer baseline submits the observed price version; the server checks its authoritative value and either honors a documented quote or asks for confirmation of the change. Cache freshness and customer consent are separate decisions.  
 Exit artifact: describe one stale-fill race on a timeline, then demonstrate how your selected mitigation preserves the stated freshness bound. Do not claim instantaneous invalidation unless every relevant race and failure path supports it. 
 Request trace: Authoritative price at purchase  A catalog request hits price version twelve; checkout submits that version; inventory checks the authoritative quote; a changed price triggers explicit reconfirmation. If invalidation is delayed, browsing may be stale but the purchase promise remains protected. Choose cache-aside for browsing because the sixty-second freshness allowance permits a bounded stale view.

title: 6. Replicate data without losing the meaning of success
text:
Copies solve different problems 
 Replication maintains multiple copies of data. It can improve read capacity and help survive a machine failure, but copies can disagree. Corner Market starts with a leader database accepting writes and replicas following its change log. A leader is the node authorized to sequence changes for a dataset. Replication lag is the delay between a leader's change and a replica applying it. A fresh reservation may therefore exist on the leader while a replica still reports no reservation. 
 Asynchronous replication acknowledges a write before a remote copy confirms it; synchronous replication waits for specified confirmation. Neither label is enough: does confirmation mean received in memory, durably written, or applied and visible? Waiting for more distant copies generally increases latency and makes success depend on more network paths. If only an asynchronous replica survives a leader crash, recently acknowledged writes may be absent. State this as a potential recovery-point loss rather than promising durability from the existence of replicas. 
 Specify a consistency guarantee 
 Consistency describes which observations a distributed system permits. Linearizability makes each operation appear to take effect at one instant between its invocation and response, respecting real-time order. Eventual consistency says replicas converge after updates stop and communication recovers; it gives no specific time bound without additional assumptions. Read-your-writes means a client observes its own acknowledged updates. These guarantees are not interchangeable and should be selected for operations, not casually attached to an entire product. 
 For a shopper immediately opening a new reservation, route that session's read to the leader, or carry a replication position and wait for a replica to catch up before serving it. The latter needs a deadline and fallback. Catalog reads may tolerate lag, while inventory decrements require one authoritative ordering. A consistent database does not make an independent cache consistent. Follow the complete response path when stating the guarantee. 
 Consensus and fencing 
 Consensus is agreement among nodes on a value or ordered sequence despite some failures. Raft uses leaders, terms, and replicated logs; a majority is central to its commit and election rules. In a five-node voting group, a majority is three, allowing progress with two unavailable nodes when the remaining nodes can communicate under the protocol's assumptions. The original  Raft paper , checked 2026-10-19, explains safety and leader election. This does not make a five-copy application automatically a correct consensus implementation. 
 During a network split, a former leader may continue running even after a new leader is elected elsewhere. Preventing two writers requires fencing: downstream storage rejects operations from obsolete leadership generations. A monotonically increasing fencing token is useful only if the resource enforces it atomically. A lock lease alone is unsafe when a process pauses beyond its lease, resumes, and writes as though it still owns the lock. Timeouts detect suspicion, not certainty of death. 
 Availability during partitions 
 A partition is a communication failure that prevents some nodes from exchanging messages. For operations requiring a single agreed stock count, a disconnected minority should reject or defer writes rather than independently selling the same last item. That sacrifices immediate write availability to preserve the chosen correctness promise. Browsing cached descriptions can continue with an explicit stale-data policy. “The service is available” is too broad when different operations intentionally behave differently. 
 Quorum arithmetic needs assumptions. With three replicas, write acknowledgments from two and reads from two have intersecting sets, but intersection alone does not ensure linearizable reads. Version selection, concurrent writes, failed partial writes, leadership, and repair behavior matter. Do not derive a guarantee solely from R + W > N. Explain the actual algorithm or rely on a documented database guarantee that matches the operation. 
 Recovery is an operational procedure 
 A replica faithfully reproduces accidental deletes, so replication is not a backup. Backups preserve recoverable historical states; test restoration, ownership, access, and replay to a target point. Failover includes detection, election or promotion, fencing, routing updates, client reconnects, and data reconciliation. Test the entire sequence. Observe lag by time and log position, last successful backup restoration, rejected stale writes, and application-visible errors during failover. 
  Practice: can an isolated store keep selling its locally cached stock?  Only if the business accepts possible overselling, or stock was previously allocated into a bounded store-owned quota that cannot overlap other sellers. A quota changes the model: each side may spend only its allocation. On reconnection, reconcile allocations and sales. Simply copying the shared stock count to both sides does not create independent ownership.  
 Exit artifact: state one read guarantee and one write guarantee, draw a partition, and identify which requests succeed, wait, or fail. Include the acknowledged data that could be lost under your selected replication policy. 
 Request trace: One accepted writer  A reserve request reaches the elected leader; its update is replicated according to the selected durability contract; only then is success returned. If the leader disappears before acknowledgment, the outcome may remain uncertain. Reuse request identity after failover and fence stale leaders so retries cannot create a second hold.

title: 7. Partition by ownership, queries, and skew
text:
Partition only when there is a pressure 
 Partitioning divides a dataset into subsets. Sharding usually means placing subsets on independently managed database nodes. A table partition inside one database can simplify retention without independently scaling every resource. Corner Market's baseline order volume does not itself justify sharding. First improve queries, indexes, archival, connection management, and vertical capacity. Partition when storage, write throughput, operational isolation, or geographic ownership has a measured requirement that one node cannot economically satisfy. 
 A partition key decides where a record belongs. Choosing store identifier keeps a store's inventory and reservations together, helping local transactions. Choosing shopper identifier makes shopper history local, but a checkout touching several stores may cross shards. Choosing random order identifier spreads writes while forcing shopper history to consult an index or multiple shards. There is no universally correct key: list the important reads, writes, transaction boundaries, and expected skew before choosing. 
 Hash and range placement 
 Hash partitioning maps a key through a function to a partition, tending to spread many unrelated keys. Range partitioning groups ordered values, helping range scans and time-based retention but risking concentrated writes to the newest range. A mapping such as hash(key) modulo node count is simple, yet changing node count remaps many keys. A directory or stable logical bucket layer decouples records from physical nodes: hash into 1,024 logical buckets, then map buckets to servers. 
 At an illustrative 2 TB dataset and 1,024 uniformly populated buckets, each bucket averages approximately 1.95 GB using decimal units. Moving sixteen buckets moves about 31.25 GB on average. Actual bucket sizes and hotness can differ dramatically. Keep both byte and request metrics per bucket; equal storage does not imply equal compute demand. Stable hashing is a placement aid, not proof that the workload is balanced. 
 Hot keys need a separate answer 
 Suppose one celebrity grocer receives forty percent of all traffic. With sixteen shards, a store-key scheme still concentrates that traffic on one shard. A hot key is a single identifier with excessive demand; a hot partition can contain many individually ordinary keys. Cache immutable reads, split large stores into item groups, or isolate the tenant. A single inventory item's strict stock counter remains a contention point unless the product supports quota allocation or queued admission. 
 Salting appends a random or chosen suffix to spread writes. It helps independent events because readers can aggregate across suffixes. It complicates unique constraints, ordered pagination, and atomic counters. “Salt the key” is therefore incomplete for stock: independently decrementing several counters requires safe initial allocation and rules for transferring unused quantity. Global unique usernames similarly need a coordinating namespace or a uniqueness mechanism beyond local shard constraints. 
 Reshard without guessing ownership 
 A migration must decide which location may accept writes at every moment. One workable outline creates a target copy, streams subsequent source changes, verifies counts and checksums at a known log position, briefly fences or redirects writes, catches up the target, then switches the routing directory version. Retain a rollback window. A dual-write phase without a durable reconciliation mechanism can leave source and target divergent whenever one write succeeds and the other fails. 
 Routing clients should learn a mapping version and handle stale routes through a bounded redirect or retry. Move requests with their idempotency identity so a retry crossing the cutover cannot create duplicate reservations. Monitor both missing records and duplicated effects. Checksums of a whole dataset may conceal which range diverged; compare per-range or per-bucket summaries and sample semantic queries as well. 
 Cross-shard behavior and privacy 
 A cross-shard join combines records stored under different owners. It can require fan-out and merging, which increases network work and exposes the request to more failures. Maintain a derived shopper-order index when that view is important, accepting and measuring its lag. A distributed transaction can preserve atomicity across participants but adds coordination and failure handling. A saga instead records a sequence of local steps with compensating actions; compensation is a business action and may not perfectly undo an external effect. 
 Deleting a shopper's data now requires discovering authoritative rows, replicas, caches, derived indexes, exports, and backup retention policies. A shard directory is operational infrastructure whose loss can make otherwise healthy data unreachable. Back up mappings, test rebuilding them, and constrain tenant access so an incorrect key cannot route a shopper into another tenant's dataset. 
  Practice: choose a shard key for inventory and explain one rejected alternative.  Start with store identifier if most reservations and replenishment are store-local. Reject shopper identifier for authoritative inventory because independent shoppers contend on the same store-item stock. Keep a separate shopper-order projection for history. Revisit the choice when a single store exceeds a shard's capacity, using item groups or explicit allocations rather than assuming more shards fix one hot item.  
 Exit artifact: draw ownership before, during, and after moving one bucket. Identify the only accepted writer in each phase and show how a stale client recovers without duplicating an effect. 
 Request trace: One owner per bucket  A reserve request hashes store s7 to bucket seventeen; routing version eight points to server B; B performs the local transaction. A stale router sends to A after cutover; A must reject or redirect rather than write. This ownership check is essential even if both databases contain apparently complete copies.

title: 8. Make asynchronous work replayable and bounded
text:
Separate accepting work from finishing it 
 Asynchronous processing records work for another process to finish later. Corner Market should not fail a committed order because email is temporarily unavailable. A queue distributes tasks to workers; a log retains an ordered sequence that consumers can read independently. Choose a task queue for sending receipts and a retained event log when analytics, search indexing, and audit projections need independent replay. “Asynchronous” does not mean instantaneous, durable, or guaranteed to succeed. 
 The response must distinguish accepted from completed. Return a stable job identifier and state such as pending, running, succeeded, or failed. Define the maximum queueing delay and how users learn about terminal failure. A worker acknowledgment tells the broker the worker has completed its obligation; acknowledge too early and a crash loses work, acknowledge too late and successful work may be repeated. Exactly which effect counts as completion needs an explicit contract. 
 The database-to-broker gap 
 If an order commits and then the process crashes before publishing its event, downstream systems never hear about the order. Publishing first has the opposite problem: consumers may see an order that later rolls back. The transactional outbox writes the order and an event row in the same database transaction. A relay publishes committed event rows and marks progress. Relay crashes can duplicate publication, so consumers must tolerate repeated event identifiers. 
  BEGIN;
INSERT INTO order_header (...);
INSERT INTO outbox (event_id, aggregate_id, kind, payload) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;
-- relay publishes only committed outbox records  
 An event is a statement about something that occurred, such as OrderConfirmed; a command requests an action, such as SendReceipt. Include event identifier, entity identifier, schema version, occurrence time, and necessary nonsecret data. Avoid copying every personal field into every event. Retention, access control, and deletion become harder as copies multiply. A schema change should tolerate older consumers during rollout. 
 Delivery and effects 
 At-least-once delivery may repeat a message; at-most-once delivery may lose it. Exactly-once claims always need a boundary. Apache Kafka documents transactional processing guarantees and the limits when interacting with external systems in its  design documentation , checked 2026-10-19. A broker transaction does not automatically make an external email or payment provider participate atomically. 
 For a local projection, insert the event identifier into a processed-events table and update the projection in one database transaction under a unique constraint. For an external effect, pass a stable provider idempotency key if the provider supports a suitable contract, or maintain an attempt record and reconcile uncertain outcomes. A worker that crashes after sending a receipt but before recording completion can send it twice on retry; accepting duplicate email may be reasonable, accepting duplicate captures is not. 
 Ordering and event time 
 A partition is an independently ordered subset of a log. Key inventory events by store-item when per-item ordering matters. There is no global order across independent partitions unless an additional mechanism creates one. Consumers must handle missing versions and out-of-order arrivals from other sources. An event's occurrence time differs from processing time. A receipt event generated offline may arrive after newer events, so a dashboard must state its policy for late data. 
 A watermark estimates event-time completeness for a processing window; it is a policy based on observed progress and lateness assumptions, not proof that no older event can ever arrive. Count orders in five-minute windows with a defined late-arrival allowance, then emit corrections or route very late events for reconciliation. Distinguish business totals from an approximate live chart so an operational dashboard does not become an accidental financial ledger. 
 Backpressure and poison messages 
 Backpressure slows or rejects producers when consumers cannot keep up. At 250 arrivals/second and 150 completions/second, backlog grows by 100/second. A large queue postpones overload; it does not create capacity. Bound queue size, prioritize critical work, limit worker concurrency, and protect downstream services. Track oldest-message age alongside queue depth because users experience delay, not abstract message counts. 
 A poison message repeatedly fails due to data or code that retries cannot fix. Retry transient failures with a bounded schedule, then isolate the item in a dead-letter queue with reason and safe inspection tools. Assign an owner and replay procedure. Replaying an entire backlog after a bug fix must preserve deduplication and downstream rate limits. Otherwise recovery becomes a second incident. 
  Practice: a consumer crashes after updating its projection but before acknowledging. What must happen on replay?  The projection update and processed-event record commit together. On replay the unique event identifier reveals prior completion, so the consumer acknowledges without repeating the update. If those writes are separate, a crash between them can still double-count or skip work.  
 Exit artifact: draw the crash points before and after each commit, publish, external call, and acknowledgment. For every point, state whether replay loses, duplicates, or safely repeats the intended effect. 
 Request trace: One projection effect per event  Order O commits with outbox event E; relay publishes E; consumer commits a count increment and E receipt together; acknowledgment is lost; E returns. The receipt prevents a second increment. Choose at-least-once transport with atomic deduplication for this projection because occasional retries are preferable to silently missing orders.

title: 9. Define reliability from the shopper outward
text:
Measure a useful outcome 
 Reliability is delivering the promised behavior despite ordinary faults and change. A  SLI  measures an outcome; a  SLO  sets its target. For Corner Market, define a good catalog request as an eligible request returning a correct, authorized result within 300 milliseconds. Separately measure successful eligible reservations and duplicate payment captures. A health check returning 200 is not proof that a shopper can complete checkout. 
 Define the denominator, observation point, exclusions, and measurement window before writing a percentage. A client-side measure includes failures before the server sees a request; server logs alone cannot count them. The  Google SRE chapter on service level objectives , checked 2026-10-19, distinguishes indicators, objectives, and agreements. The objectives here are illustrative teaching choices, not recommended universal targets. 
 Budgets and dependency arithmetic 
 If 600,000 eligible checkout requests occur in a thirty-day window, a 99.9 percent request-success objective permits 600 bad requests. A time-based 99.9 percent objective over thirty days permits 43.2 minutes of failure because 30 × 24 × 60 × 0.001 = 43.2. Request and time budgets differ when traffic is uneven. Do not interchange them. An error budget is the allowed imperfection implied by the objective; it supports explicit release and reliability decisions. 
 Suppose a request requires three independently available dependencies, each available 99.9 percent of the time. Under that simplifying independence assumption, all three are available approximately 0.999 cubed, or 99.7003 percent. Shared network or identity failures violate independence and may be worse. Reduce required dependencies by making email asynchronous, storing necessary local state, or degrading optional recommendations. Replicating every component without examining shared failure causes can leave the same weakness intact. 
 Prevent overload from becoming collapse 
 A timeout caps waiting; a circuit breaker temporarily stops calls to a failing dependency; a bulkhead limits one class of work so it cannot exhaust all resources. Configure each around the customer contract. Bound database connection pools and request queues. When the system is saturated, reject some new work promptly with retry guidance rather than allowing every request to time out while consuming memory. Retried work is still work: three retries can multiply offered traffic precisely when capacity is weakest. 
 Degradation should be intentional. Serve a cached product description with visible freshness when allowed, omit optional recommendations, and disable new checkout if inventory correctness cannot be preserved. Avoid returning “order failed” after a payment timeout when the actual outcome is unknown. Persist a pending state and reconcile. Make support tools able to locate the attempt by a nonsecret identifier. 
 Observe causes and consequences 
 Metrics are numerical measurements over time; logs are individual event records; traces connect steps across a request. Track request rate, errors, duration, saturation, database lock waits, replica lag, queue age, and business invariant violations. Use stable correlation identifiers without embedding personal data. High-cardinality labels such as raw shopper identifiers can overwhelm metric systems and expose sensitive information. Sample traces carefully so rare errors and slow paths remain diagnosable. 
 Alert on user impact or imminent loss of a critical promise. A high CPU reading may be healthy utilization; a rising duplicate-capture count deserves immediate attention even when CPU is low. Build runbooks with safe first actions, verification queries, escalation ownership, and rollback instructions. Run a restore exercise and a dependency-outage exercise before claiming recovery readiness. A backup job's success signal is weaker evidence than a verified restoration. 
 Security belongs in the data flow 
 Identify trust boundaries: client to gateway, service to database, workers to payment provider, and operator to administration tools. Authenticate identity, authorize each object access, encrypt transport, minimize stored secrets, and grant each service only necessary permissions. Treat uploaded files and search text as untrusted input. Validate content and size; avoid using unchecked user input as a network destination. An upload service fetching an arbitrary URL can become a path into private networks. 
 Keep public catalog data separate from private orders. Redact credentials and payment details from logs. Define retention and deletion policies with qualified business and legal owners rather than inventing universal compliance rules. Audit privileged actions and test revoked access. A design diagram should show both ordinary traffic and administrative paths because maintenance interfaces often bypass assumptions made for the public API. 
  Practice: checkout availability improves, but support sees more charged-without-order complaints. Is the release successful?  No conclusion follows from availability alone. Investigate the payment/order invariant, uncertain attempts, and reconciliation lag. A faster acknowledgment that hides an inconsistent business outcome can improve a narrow metric while harming shoppers. Rollback or disable the risky path based on the correctness impact.  
 Exit artifact: define two user-facing indicators and one invariant alarm, then explain the first five minutes of response to each breach. 
 Request trace: Authorized recovery  A shopper requests order O; the service checks identity and O ownership before reading details; a database timeout triggers bounded retry. If an operator later investigates, the support path must enforce its own permission and audit checks. Reliability recovery never grants permission to expose another shopper’s order.

title: 10. Add regions only with a recovery and ownership plan
text:
Geography changes the problem 
 A region is a geographic deployment area containing infrastructure with some shared failure risks. An availability zone is an isolation area within a region under a provider's documented model. Neither term guarantees independence from all identity, networking, software, or operational failures. Corner Market starts in one city with a deployment spanning local failure domains. Another region is justified by a geographic latency requirement, a disaster-recovery objective, a residency constraint, or a business need for regional isolation. 
 Active-passive means one region normally serves writes while another is prepared to take over. Active-active means multiple regions serve work concurrently, but it does not specify who may write the same record. Assigning each store a home region lets many regions be active while each inventory item retains one writer. Routing an inventory reservation across a long-distance link adds latency; accepting local writes everywhere instead creates a conflict-resolution problem. 
 Recovery objectives are contracts 
  RTO  states a restoration-time target.  RPO  states tolerated data loss. Assume an illustrative thirty-minute RTO and five-minute RPO for catalog administration; payment records may require a stricter contract. A backup every day cannot by itself satisfy five-minute RPO. Continuous log shipping might support that goal only if shipping, retention, credentials, restoration, and replay are tested together. 
 Break recovery into detection, decision, fencing the old writer, data promotion or restore, traffic movement, dependency reconnection, and validation. If these take 3 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 2 + 3 + 4 minutes, total recovery is 27 minutes, leaving little margin under a thirty-minute objective. DNS caching, stuck clients, or missing secrets can consume the margin. Recovery drills should measure the shopper-visible endpoint, not just the moment a database starts. 
 Resolve ownership before conflicts 
 During a regional partition, two writable copies cannot both independently promise the last apple to different customers while preserving a single shared stock invariant. Options include a single reachable owner, prior regional quota allocation, or an explicit oversell policy. Last-write-wins reconciliation discards one update based on an ordering rule; that may be acceptable for a cosmetic preference but cannot undo a fulfilled purchase. Timestamps also carry clock uncertainty and are not proof of causal order. 
 Failback is a second migration. After the old region returns, do not simply reopen writes there. Determine which region is authoritative, reconcile changes, rebuild or catch up replicas, verify state, then move traffic under controlled ownership. Test what happens when the original region returns while automation is still promoting the standby. Human approval may be part of a business recovery procedure, but its staffing and decision time belong in the RTO model. 
 Cost is a model with uncertainty 
 Estimate total operating cost as compute plus storage plus requests plus network transfer plus managed-service charges plus operational effort. Use current provider pricing when making a real purchasing decision; these examples deliberately avoid invented dollar prices. The catalog baseline transfers 4 GB/day before images. If an image variant adds an average 200 KB to each of two million daily page loads, that adds 400 GB/day. Media caching may matter more financially than optimizing a small orders table. 
 Replication multiplies stored copies, cross-region transfer, and operational testing. More services multiply deployment coordination and on-call knowledge. A managed database may cost more directly while reducing recovery and maintenance effort; quantify the staffing assumption rather than pretending engineering time is free. A cheaper design that cannot satisfy the correctness contract is not an equivalent alternative. Conversely, five-nines availability is wasteful if no user or business requirement funds its consequences. 
 Evolve through reversible steps 
 Use an expand-migrate-contract change: add a compatible new field or store, populate historical data, run both readers or compare outputs, switch traffic gradually, then remove the old path after evidence supports removal. Shadow reads compare a new implementation without making it authoritative. A canary release exposes a small traffic fraction to a change, with meaningful rollback signals. These techniques need representative traffic; a canary that never touches the rare payment path cannot validate that path. 
 Write a migration ledger: current owner, desired owner, cutover conditions, rollback conditions, data reconciliation, and the last reversible point. Some external actions, such as sending a shipment, cannot be undone by deploying old code. Separate a code rollback from a data repair or business compensation. Feature flags should have owners and removal dates so temporary branches do not become permanent architecture. 
  Practice: management asks for active-active because a region outage is frightening. What evidence do you bring?  Bring the specific customer impact, required RTO/RPO, measured current recovery time, ownership model, and estimated complexity and cost of alternatives. Compare tested active-passive recovery against partitioned active-active writes. If each store has one home writer, explain how cross-region customers behave during home-region loss. Do not promise universal write availability while concealing correctness compromises.  
 Exit artifact: rehearse a regional loss and a failback using a timed checklist. Every recovery objective should map to a demonstrated procedure or an explicitly recorded gap. 
 Request trace: One regional inventory owner  A shopper in region B reserves an item owned by region A; B forwards to A and waits within a deadline. A partition occurs after A commits. B reports pending and reconciles using the same request identity. It must not independently repeat the decrement against a writable regional copy.

title: 11. Implement the boundary: Python and low-level design
text:
Make the promise executable 
 Low-level design turns system promises into interfaces, data structures, state transitions, and tests. Start with one narrow component rather than a hierarchy of speculative classes. Corner Market needs a reservation service whose public operation either creates one hold, returns the existing result for a repeated request, or explains a business rejection. Inject a clock so expiry tests do not sleep, and inject persistence so concurrency assumptions are visible. An in-memory implementation teaches interfaces but is not evidence of distributed correctness. 
  from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReserveCommand:
    shopper_id: str
    request_key: str
    store_id: str
    item_id: str
    quantity: int

class ReservationRepository(Protocol):
    def reserve_once(self, command: ReserveCommand, now: float) -> str:
        """Atomically deduplicate, check stock, and create one hold."""
        ...

class ReservationService:
    def __init__(self, repository, clock):
        self.repository = repository
        self.clock = clock

    def reserve(self, command):
        if not 1 <= command.quantity <= 100:
            raise ValueError("quantity outside supported range")
        return self.repository.reserve_once(command, self.clock())  
 The repository contract is deliberately strong: it must implement all listed effects atomically, compare repeated request bodies, and return the original result when appropriate. Splitting these into independent repository calls would leak a race into the service. A production implementation uses a database transaction and unique constraint, not a Python dictionary shared by several servers. Use wall-clock timestamps for business deadlines, with a documented authority; use a monotonic clock for local elapsed durations so clock adjustments do not refill tokens backward. 
 Exercise one: deterministic token bucket 
 A token bucket admits bursts while limiting sustained request rate. It stores capacity, refill rate, available tokens, and last observed time. On each request, compute elapsed time, refill up to capacity, then spend one token if available. With capacity ten and refill two tokens/second, an idle bucket admits ten immediate requests; an eleventh is rejected; after half a second one token is available. The check and decrement must be atomic under concurrent callers. 
  Reveal implementation outline and tests  Use  tokens = min(capacity, tokens + max(0, now - last) * rate) ; update the effective last time without allowing it to move backward; spend only when tokens are at least one. Inject a monotonic clock. Test initial burst, fractional refill, cap after long idle, simultaneous calls, and backward-time input to the pure model. For multiple servers, either centrally coordinate updates or explicitly accept a bounded per-instance overshoot. A process-local lock protects threads in one process, not a fleet.  
 Exercise two: a reservation state machine 
 Model states HELD, CONFIRMED, and EXPIRED. A transition function takes the current state, command, authoritative time, and deadline. Confirm succeeds only while held and before the deadline; expire succeeds only while held and at or after it. Repeating a completed operation returns its stable result. Two concurrent operations must compare and update the version atomically. Choose the exact deadline boundary and apply it consistently rather than letting two code paths disagree about equality. 
  Reveal critical scenarios  Test confirm just before expiry, expire exactly at the deadline, confirm after expiry, repeated expire, repeated confirm, and a confirm-versus-expire race. Assert that quantity is returned at most once and cannot be both confirmed and returned. A transaction or compare-and-swap against the same reservation version chooses one winner. A test that only calls methods sequentially does not validate the race.  
 Exercise three: bounded asynchronous workers 
 Use a bounded  asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)  and a fixed worker count to avoid creating one task per unbounded incoming item. A queue's  put  waits when its configured capacity is exhausted, and  task_done  and  join  support tracking completed queue work. Those mechanics are documented in  Python's asyncio queues , checked 2026-10-19. The queue is process-local and does not survive a crash. 
  Reveal implementation review criteria  Each worker gets an item, performs a bounded operation, and calls task_done in a finally block after deliberately handling the outcome. task_done is queue bookkeeping, not proof of business success or a durable acknowledgment. On failure or cancellation, persist a terminal outcome or arrange an explicit retry/requeue before treating the work as handled; blindly calling it and discarding the exception can silently lose work. Handle cancellation and shutdown deliberately. Distinguish an attempted job from a successful business effect. Test a slow dependency, a failing item, a full queue, and shutdown with work pending. If durable delivery is required, replace the process-local queue with a persistent broker and preserve the acknowledgment and deduplication contract.  
 Design review before abstraction 
 Prefer explicit domain results such as OutOfStock, PriceChanged, and PendingPayment over catching every exception as “failed.” Separate validation, persistence, and external side effects so tests can target boundaries. Use composition when behavior varies, such as a retry policy or clock; avoid adding factories and inheritance only to decorate a simple function. Explain thread safety, process safety, and distributed safety separately. Each has a different sharing boundary. 
 Exit artifact: implement all three exercises locally, add meaningful race and failure tests, and explain one guarantee your code does not provide. The snippets are teaching contracts, not a deployable payment implementation. Passing unit tests demonstrates the tested model; it does not establish database, network, or regional behavior that the model omitted. 
 Predict the confirm-versus-expire race  Reservation R is HELD at version four. Confirm reads HELD just before the deadline; expiry reads HELD at the deadline; expiry changes R to EXPIRED and returns three units; confirm blindly changes R to CONFIRMED. Now the system sold stock it already returned. Require both operations to condition their transition on the same authoritative state and version, within the transaction that changes inventory. Only one wins. Define the deadline comparison using a shared clock policy, and treat a losing confirmation as a business rejection rather than overwriting the winning state.

title: 12. Practice principal-level decisions and demonstrate mastery
text:
Move from a plausible diagram to an accountable choice 
 A principal engineer explains why a design fits a business, how teams will change it safely, and which evidence would overturn the choice. Corner Market has grown from a city pilot into several independently operated markets. A recommendation to split the application must name the bottleneck: conflicting ownership, release coupling, scaling pressure, regulatory boundaries, or operational blast radius. “Microservices scale” is not a decision argument. A modular application can preserve clear ownership until separate deployment has a concrete benefit. 
 An architecture decision record captures context, options, choice, consequences, and revisit triggers. Keep the consequence specific: one store owns inventory writes, so distant shoppers pay an extra network trip; in return the last-item invariant is easier to protect. A useful revisit trigger is measured checkout latency exceeding the agreed objective for a sustained interval, rather than a vague intention to “scale later.” Include migration cost, staffing, and recovery practice alongside infrastructure capability. 
 Practice case: search is late, checkout is correct 
 Prompt: catalog updates appear in search several minutes late, and product leadership asks for instant search and instant checkout everywhere. Clarify the observed lag distribution, which fields need freshness, geographic scope, and whether “instant” means a specific percentile. Assume product descriptions may lag sixty seconds, deletion from public search must propagate within that bound, and price is revalidated at checkout. The first task is to locate delay: outbox age, broker lag, indexing throughput, refresh timing, or client cache. 
 Do not replace the search engine before measuring the pipeline. If indexing workers are saturated, scale them within storage capacity and apply backpressure; if invalidations are missing, fix event reliability. Serve authoritative details when a result opens and handle deleted items gracefully. For a hard removal promise, a query-time suppression list or authoritative permission check may be required while indexes catch up. That adds a dependency and must itself meet availability and latency requirements. 
  Reveal a strong answer and a weak answer  A strong answer separates search discovery freshness from checkout correctness, proposes measurements at each boundary, and identifies the smallest compatible fix. It states what users see during lag and how removal requests are verified. A weak answer adds a cache to an already stale path, or promises globally instant indexing without a latency budget and failure policy.  
 Practice case: shared platform versus team autonomy 
 Prompt: three teams each built a job scheduler; leadership proposes a single company-wide scheduler. Clarify task volume, deadlines, execution duration, isolation needs, retry semantics, and incident ownership. Shared infrastructure can remove duplicate maintenance but concentrates failure and couples migrations. Separate control-plane functions, such as schedule storage and dispatch policy, from execution environments where tenant workloads run. A control plane manages configuration and coordination; a data plane performs the actual user work. 
 Propose an adoption path: standardize task identifiers and result states first, onboard a low-risk workload, verify fairness and recovery, then migrate critical tasks with dual observation. Keep tenant quotas and resource isolation so one customer's backlog does not starve another. Define who owns a misbehaving task, who operates the scheduler, and who can pause a tenant. Reject a forced simultaneous rewrite because it creates a large irreversible coordination event without proving the platform's fitness. 
  Reveal the important tradeoff  A shared scheduler is valuable when it offers a better reliability contract and lower total operating effort than the existing systems. It is costly when teams need incompatible execution guarantees or no team can operate it. A principal answer proposes evidence, staged adoption, and clear ownership rather than equating standardization with universal centralization.  
 Choose a learning path 
 A beginner should complete foundations one through five, implement the low-level exercises, and solve URL shortening before adding replication and partitioning. A backend practitioner should begin with the estimates and transaction exercises, then attempt correctness-heavy reservations, payments, and scheduling. A data or AI architect should still complete request-path and transactional reasoning, then emphasize streams, analytics, feature freshness, and model-serving failure modes. A principal interview path adds migration, multi-region ownership, cost, organizational constraints, and adversarial follow-ups to every worked case. 
 Use deliberate practice rather than reading every sample first. Attempt a prompt for forty-five minutes, record assumptions and unresolved questions, then open the concealed answer. Change one condition: tenfold traffic, an unavailable region, a malicious tenant, or a stricter invariant. Explain which part of your design changes and which remains justified. Repeating the same diagram from memory demonstrates recall; adapting it with explicit consequences demonstrates transferable understanding. 
 Assess evidence, not page completion 
 Score each attempt from zero to three on requirement clarity, quantitative reasoning, data correctness, failure analysis, tradeoff depth, and communication. Zero means absent; one means named without mechanism; two means coherent under stated assumptions; three means defended under a changed assumption with a recovery or migration plan. Keep the original attempt so improvement is observable. Reading completion and quiz scores are useful study signals, but neither certifies mastery or guarantees an interview outcome. 
  Final oral drill: your preferred database is unavailable for six hours. What do you do?  First clarify whether this is a new-design constraint or an incident. During an incident, preserve invariants, stop unsafe writes, expose pending outcomes, use tested recovery, and communicate measured impact. For a new design, revisit requirements and compare alternatives by transactions, query patterns, recovery, team skill, and migration. Naming a different product without reconstructing its guarantees is not a complete answer.  
 Exit artifact: maintain three independently attempted cases, one implemented concurrency exercise, one failure rehearsal, and one written decision record with a rejected alternative. Ask a peer to challenge assumptions and record the feedback. Treat remaining uncertainties as a practice backlog with concrete experiments, not as an excuse to add unmotivated components.

title: Case 1 · Share a neighborhood listing
text:
Build the smallest reliable doorway into Corner Market, a fictional neighborhood marketplace. This case trains requirement selection, key allocation, caching, and abuse handling. All numbers are interview assumptions, not claims about a real business. 
 Exact interview prompt  Design a URL shortener so sellers can share Corner Market listings. Explain how you avoid duplicate codes, keep redirects fast, and remove dangerous links. 
 Clarify before drawing  Ask: arbitrary websites or only our listings? Assume both, with malware controls. Can destinations change? Assume immutable destinations; owners may disable links. Are aliases required? Optional custom aliases are in scope. Anonymous creation? No; authenticated sellers only. Is a short link a secret? No. Do we need exact click counts? Approximate daily analytics suffice. Retain mappings for one year. A removed or expired code is never reassigned within the retention period. 
 Set nonfunctional requirements: redirect service availability objective 99.95% monthly, redirect server-side p95 latency under 100 ms in the primary region, and owner creation response p95 under 300 ms. A percentile means the stated fraction of observations fall below that value. These are proposed objectives to validate with the interviewer and load tests; network time is separate. Disable propagation must complete within 60 seconds, so cache policy is part of the correctness contract. 
 Estimate with units  Assume 1 million new links/day and 100 million redirects/day; decimal units throughout. Average creation rate is 1,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 11.6 writes/s.
