Redirect rate is approximately 1,157/s. With an assumed 10× peak, provision and test 116 writes/s and 11,574 redirects/s. A 500-byte logical mapping costs 500 MB/day, or 182.5 GB/year before indexes, replicas, database overhead, and backups. Three complete copies alone require 547.5 GB. A 90% cache hit rate leaves about 1,158 peak database reads/s, but a cold cache must survive much more. 
 Use 10 random base62 characters: 62 choices per character gives 62 10  ≈ 8.39 × 10 17  possible codes. At 365 million stored links, the approximate probability that a fresh candidate collides is n/N ≈ 4.35 × 10 −10 . This does not mean no collision ever occurs; birthday effects accumulate across all draws. A unique database constraint, with bounded retry on conflict, is the actual guarantee. 
 Contract and data model   POST /v1/links
Idempotency-Key: seller-generated-request-id
{ "destination": "https://example.test/item/42", "alias": null }
201 { "code": "k8W1pZ3aQx", "short_url": "https://s.example.test/k8W1pZ3aQx" }
GET /k8W1pZ3aQx  → 302, Location: validated destination
DELETE /v1/links/k8W1pZ3aQx → 204 (owner only)

links(code PRIMARY KEY, owner_id, destination, status,
      created_at, expires_at, version)
requests(owner_id, idempotency_key, request_hash, code,
         UNIQUE(owner_id, idempotency_key))  
 An idempotency key identifies one intended operation across retries. Store its response and request hash in the same transaction as the mapping; a reused key with different input returns conflict. Let the database decide alias uniqueness atomically. Checking availability then inserting is vulnerable to two concurrent requests. 
 Labeled architecture and progressive design  CREATE: Seller → API/auth → mapping database + request record
REDIRECT: Browser → edge/load balancer → redirect service → cache
                                                  miss ↓
                                             mapping database
ANALYTICS: redirect service → bounded event buffer → daily aggregation
DISABLE: Owner → API → status update → invalidation + expiry fallback 
 First deliver a single service and relational database with an indexed primary-key lookup. Add multiple stateless redirect instances when measured demand warrants them. A cache stores frequently requested mappings for at most 30 seconds. A time to live (TTL) is the maximum cache residence duration. Always check expiry and status in cached data. Use short-lived negative caching for missing codes to reduce random-code attacks, but invalidate negative entries when a custom alias is created. Never let analytics determine whether the redirect succeeds. 
 Choose a temporary 302 redirect and explicit cache directives because owners can disable links. A permanent redirect may remain cached in clients beyond your purge control. The 60-second disable promise requires bounding every participating cache, including an edge cache if added. Sensitive or urgent takedowns may need a small denylist checked before normal cache lookup. Explain the availability cost of making that check authoritative. 
 Deep dives and failure analysis  A viral link is a hot key: one key receives a disproportionate share of requests. Replicating that small mapping across service caches reduces database load; merely sharding the database does not spread reads for one code. Coalesce concurrent misses so one request loads a mapping and others wait briefly. Randomize refresh times without extending the maximum takedown budget. A stale cache cannot prove that a link remains non-revoked: never extend an entry beyond the stated revocation deadline without checking the authority. Include replica lag and refill races in that deadline; use versioned invalidation or authoritative revocation checks if the required bound cannot otherwise be met. Negative lookup traffic still needs per-client limits and bounded cache admission. 
 On a database outage, serve eligible cached mappings until their allowed lifetime expires; return a retryable 503 for unknown mappings rather than falsely saying they do not exist. A read replica can reduce load but replication lag may make a newly created link appear absent; route recent creation reads to the primary or seed cache after commit, with a primary fallback on a miss. A cache outage must trigger concurrency limits, not an uncontrolled database stampede. 
 Do not fetch arbitrary destinations synchronously from unrestricted servers. Validate supported schemes, reject control characters, use safe redirect header construction, and isolate any malware fetcher with network restrictions against internal addresses and redirects to them. This prevents server-side request forgery when a scanner visits attacker-chosen URLs. Track abuse reports and audit disable actions without logging secret query strings unnecessarily. 
 Alternatives, operations, and evolution  A monotonically increasing integer encoded in base62 is simpler but exposes enumeration; adding obscurity is not authorization. Hashing the long URL does not remove collisions and creates policy questions about ownership and destination normalization. A global distributed key service is unnecessary for this workload unless allocation becomes a measured bottleneck. Start in one write region with backups and restore drills; multi-region reads can follow. Multi-region writes need collision enforcement and an explicit conflict policy for custom aliases. 
 Monitor redirect success and latency, cache hit rate, primary fallback rate, collision retries, disable propagation, and analytics event loss. Sample logs; billions of full request logs can cost more than mappings. Add capacity before cache cold-start tests exceed the database budget. Partition old mappings by retention only after examining lookup and expiration costs. 
 Interviewer follow-ups and rubric   Practice: two sellers request the same alias at the same time. What happens?  The unique constraint accepts one transaction. The loser receives 409 and can choose another alias. Its idempotency record must not claim success. Retrying the winner's original key returns the original response.    Practice: analytics must become billing-grade. What changes?  Define which redirects count, durable event acceptance, stable event IDs, deduplication, reconciliation, and an explicit behavior when the event path is unavailable. The earlier lossy buffer no longer meets requirements.    Strong answer:  ties temporary redirects and TTL to revocation, calculates rates, distinguishes collision probability from uniqueness enforcement, and bounds cache failures.  Weak answer:  says “use Redis and hashing” without atomic allocation, deletion behavior, or an overload plan. Principal depth includes abuse ownership, regional failure policy, and measurable rollout criteria. 
 Technical reference checked 2026-10-19:  PostgreSQL constraints  for atomic uniqueness;  HTTP semantics, RFC 9110  for redirect behavior. The workload and design choices above are original assumptions.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  Must takedown be immediate, or may cached links resolve briefly?  Interviewer:  Assume a 60-second maximum.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  Why not use a permanent redirect for performance?  Candidate:  A browser may retain it beyond our takedown control. I choose a temporary redirect and bounded cache policy, including refill and replica lag. If you change the requirement to immediate takedown, I must validate revocation authoritatively on each resolution or use a delivery layer that can enforce the new contract.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Case 2 · A useful neighborhood feed
text:
Corner Market now lets residents follow sellers and neighborhood groups. A feed is a prepared or computed list of candidate posts. The central choice is when to do the work: when someone publishes or when someone reads. 
 Exact interview prompt  Design a home feed showing recent posts from followed sellers and groups. Handle a few accounts with millions of followers without making normal publishing slow. 
 Clarifying questions and assumed answers  Ask whether the feed is chronological or personalized. Start with reverse chronological order; introduce relevance later. Assume 1 million daily active users, 100 followed authors per user on average, public posts with block and takedown rules, 30-day feed history, and 20 cards/page. Users publish 0.2 posts/day on average. A daily active user is one who uses the app that day; it is not the number simultaneously connected. Exclude comments and ads from the first design. A new post may take five seconds to appear, but blocked or deleted content must be filtered at read time. Freshness and visibility correctness have different requirements. 
 Propose feed p95 server latency under 250 ms and 99.9% monthly availability, with graceful stale results during fanout failure. Fanout means distributing one post reference into many recipients' inboxes. Publishing must acknowledge after durable storage without waiting for every recipient. No promise of an exact immutable feed snapshot across changing moderation rules. 
 Capacity and its implications  At 1 million users × 20 page requests/day, there are 20 million page reads/day, about 231.5/s average and 2,315/s at assumed 10× peak. At 20 cards/page this is 400 million card impressions/day. Publication volume is 200,000 posts/day ≈ 2.31/s average. If each author has 100 recipients on average, push fanout produces 20 million inbox inserts/day ≈ 231.5/s average; retention of 30 days gives 600 million references. At 32 logical bytes/reference that is 19.2 GB before indexes, storage layout, and replicas. These averages hide the important tail: one author with 2 million followers produces 2 million inserts per post. 
 At an explicitly assumed sustained worker throughput of 10,000 inserts/s across a pool, that one post requires 200 seconds, exceeding five-second freshness. This is a planning calculation, not a benchmark. It motivates separating high-fanout authors or changing worker capacity; it does not prove one database technology is slow. 
 API, schema, and labeled diagram   POST /v1/posts { text, attachment_ids, client_request_id }
GET /v1/feed?cursor=opaque-token&limit=20
→ { items: [...], next_cursor, generated_at, freshness_seconds }
PUT /v1/follows/{author_id}    DELETE /v1/follows/{author_id}

posts(post_id PRIMARY KEY, author_id, created_at, body, status, version)
follows(follower_id, author_id, UNIQUE(follower_id, author_id))
inbox(user_id, created_at, post_id, PRIMARY KEY(user_id, post_id))
outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, post_id, event_type, dispatched_at)
read index: inbox(user_id, created_at DESC, post_id DESC)  
 Publish API → transaction: posts + outbox
                               ↓ dispatcher (retryable)
                         queue → fanout workers → user inboxes
                                                   ↑
Feed API → merge(user inbox, recent high-fanout author posts)
         → batch-load posts → current visibility filter → response
Follow graph ─────────────→ recipient lookup / read-time author set 
 Progressive design  Start with pull: on a feed request, query recent posts for followed authors using an index beginning with author_id and ordered by time. Merge a bounded number of recent results. This avoids copying data and is easy to reason about. Measure the cost of following hundreds or thousands of authors before moving to push fanout. 
 Then push references, not duplicated post bodies, into active users' inboxes. An outbox is a table of pending integration events written in the same database transaction as domain data. A dispatcher sends its rows to a queue. If it crashes after sending but before marking dispatched, it sends again; unique (user_id, post_id) makes repeated inserts harmless. Persist an event cursor so fanout can resume after a partial recipient batch. 
 Use a hybrid for large authors: read their latest posts at request time and merge with the materialized inbox. Materialized means precomputed and stored. Choose the threshold from estimated recipient write cost, audience activity, freshness budget, and measured read cost, not a magical follower count. Deduplicate by post_id because migration between modes can put a post in both paths. New follows need a bounded history backfill; unfollows should be checked when reading until old references are removed. 
 Pagination and visibility deep dive  Order by (created_at, post_id), with post_id as a deterministic tie-breaker. An opaque signed cursor contains that pair and a feed session cutoff time. Request the next page strictly older than the last pair and not newer than the cutoff. Offset pagination shifts when new posts arrive and repeats items. A keyset cursor avoids that shift, although deleting or hiding posts can still shorten pages; oversample within a bounded limit and report exhaustion honestly. 
 Never treat a stale inbox reference as permission to show content. Batch-load current post status and evaluate blocks, group membership, and privacy. If the authorization dependency fails, fail closed for restricted content. For public content, the interviewer must approve any bounded stale policy. Deletions create tombstones, small records indicating removed content, and trigger asynchronous cleanup; read filtering provides the immediate correctness barrier. 
 Failures and operational tradeoffs  When the queue falls behind, durable posts still exist, so show a freshness indicator and optionally fall back to a bounded pull query. Put a budget on fallback concurrency: a queue incident should not become a database incident. When one account causes enormous fanout, isolate its work so ordinary authors are not starved. Retry with backoff, cap attempts, and move persistently failing events to a review queue with an audited replay procedure. 
 If the cache disappears, reduce page size or shed optional enrichment before increasing database pressure. If the follow graph is partitioned across stores, graph changes and fanout race: a post may arrive after an unfollow, which is why read-time filtering remains necessary. Store only the 30-day window, prune inactive inboxes, and reconstruct on return when write savings justify it. 
 Alternatives and evolution  Reject push-to-everyone as the universal design because celebrity writes dominate. Reject pull-everything as the universal design when wide follow graphs and repeated reads exceed the request budget. Neither is inherently wrong at small scale. A relevance model changes pagination: scores and candidate sets evolve, so freeze a ranked result window or use a session token rather than pretending time order still suffices. Keep a chronological fallback and measure relevance quality separately from system availability. 
 Monitor feed latency, end-to-end freshness, fanout backlog age, duplicate suppression, empty-feed rate, filtered-card rate, and per-author skew. Audit privacy failures as correctness incidents. Compare cost per thousand pages and per published post as traffic grows. Roll out hybrid changes by cohort and verify no missing or repeated posts with shadow reads. 
 Follow-ups and answer rubric   Practice: a user follows an author while their post is being fanned out. Must the post appear?  Define semantics first. Our assumed policy shows the author's recent public posts after follow. Backfill plus read-time merging covers the race; deduplicate IDs. A stricter publish-time membership snapshot would require versioned graph semantics.    Practice: a deleted post appears on page two from an old cursor.  The cursor determines ordering, not authorization. Current visibility filtering must remove the post on every page and every cache path.    Strong:  derives hybrid fanout from skew, specifies resumable/idempotent work, and separates freshness from privacy.  Weak:  draws a queue without replay behavior, says “eventual consistency” to excuse deleted content, or uses offsets without discussing shifting pages. Principal depth includes cohort migration, per-tenant isolation, and cost/freshness controls. 
 Technical reference checked 2026-10-19:  PostgreSQL unique constraints . Cursor, hybrid fanout, freshness targets, and workload figures are design assumptions rather than vendor guarantees.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  Is the five-second freshness target also a promise to immediately hide blocked content?  Interviewer:  Freshness may lag, but blocked content must be hidden.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  Your inbox already contains the post. Is deleting the source enough?  Candidate:  No. The inbox is a derived list of IDs, not an authorization authority. I filter visibility at serving time and remove stale references asynchronously. If the authority is unavailable, I omit uncertain content rather than expose it. Feed completeness can degrade while the access boundary holds.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Case 3 · Buyer and seller chat
text:
A buyer asks whether a bicycle is available. A duplicate message is annoying; acknowledging a message and then losing it damages trust. This case separates durable acceptance, delivery, reading, and connection state. 
 Exact interview prompt  Design one-to-one buyer–seller messaging for Corner Market, including offline delivery, retries, read receipts, and multiple devices. Explain what “message sent” means during failures. 
 Clarifying questions and assumed answers  Assume private conversations between two members, text plus references to previously scanned attachments, history retained for one year, and no large group chat. End-to-end encryption is a possible later product requirement, not silently promised by transport encryption. Ask whether edited messages and deletion are required; support tombstone deletion but defer editing. Messages need order within one conversation; no global order across all conversations. Presence can be stale and must not authorize access. 
 Set durable-send acknowledgment p95 under 300 ms, online delivery p95 under one second under healthy conditions, and 99.95% monthly send availability. Acknowledgment means committed to the chosen durable replicated store. “Delivered” means at least one recipient device acknowledged receipt; “read” means the user explicitly advanced a read position. State that replication policy determines the remaining loss window after a regional disaster. Do not imply that a successful network write is durable storage. 
 Calculate load and connection resources  Assume 200,000 daily messaging users sending 20 messages each: 4 million messages/day, or 46.3/s average and 463/s at a 10× assumed peak. At 1,000 logical bytes/message, history adds 4 GB/day and 1.46 TB/year before indexes and replicas. Attachment bytes live in object storage and are excluded. Suppose 50,000 simultaneous devices hold connections; at an assumed 20 KB application state each, that is 1 GB of connection state across gateways, excluding operating-system socket buffers and runtime overhead. 
 With one heartbeat every 30 seconds/device, the service handles about 1,667 heartbeat sends/s and corresponding replies. Heartbeats can exceed average message traffic. Capacity testing must include reconnect storms, TLS handshakes, slow consumers, and file-descriptor limits. TLS is transport layer security, which encrypts a connection; it does not encrypt data from the service itself. 
 API and storage contract   POST /v1/conversations/{id}/messages
{ client_message_id, text, attachment_ids }
→ { message_id, sequence, accepted_at }
GET /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?after_sequence=123&limit=50
PUT /v1/conversations/{id}/read-position { sequence: 130 }
WebSocket events: message_available, delivery_receipt, presence_hint

conversations(id PRIMARY KEY, member_a, member_b, next_sequence)
messages(conversation_id, sequence, message_id, sender_id,
         client_message_id, payload, created_at, status,
         PRIMARY KEY(conversation_id, sequence),
         UNIQUE(conversation_id, sender_id, client_message_id))
read_positions(conversation_id, user_id, sequence)
outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, conversation_id, sequence)  
 A WebSocket is a persistent bidirectional connection established through an HTTP handshake. It reduces repeated connection overhead but provides no durable history by itself. The same logical send endpoint can be exposed over HTTP or a socket command; it must enforce identical authorization and deduplication. 
 Labeled architecture and progression  Devices → authenticated gateway → message service
                                  ↓ transaction
                      conversation sequence + message + outbox
                                                ↓ dispatcher
                                      delivery event queue
                                                ↓
                                     recipient gateway(s)
                                                ↓
                                      device acknowledgment
Offline/reconnect → history API → durable messages after cursor 
 Begin with HTTP sends and polling history. For each send, check current membership, then lock/update the conversation row and allocate its next sequence in the same transaction as insertion. This gives one authoritative order per conversation, not a wall-clock guess. A retry with the same client_message_id returns the existing result; different payload with that ID is conflict. A rollback must roll back allocation too, although clients should not assume every system promises gap-free sequences. 
 Add a transactional outbox and delivery workers, then connection gateways when polling cost or latency justifies them. Gateway registration maps a device to its current gateway with an expiry and connection generation. The durable store remains authoritative. After reconnect, the client fetches messages after its last stored sequence, even if the gateway believes nothing was missed. 
 Ordering, duplicates, and receipts  Delivery is at least once: messages may repeat after retries. Devices merge by stable message_id or conversation sequence and render one copy. Concurrent sends from two devices receive an order at the authoritative conversation owner. If sequence 132 arrives before 131, buffer briefly or fetch the missing range; do not reorder by client timestamps, which can be inaccurate or manipulated. A single busy conversation is serialized by design. Partitioning by conversation_id scales many conversations, but does not make one conversation infinitely scalable. 
 Read position updates are monotonic: store max(existing, requested), after verifying the position belongs to that conversation and is valid. A slow device cannot move it backward. Delivery and read receipts are separate: receiving a background push notification does not prove reading. Push notification payloads should avoid private message bodies unless product privacy policy explicitly permits them. 
 Failure analysis  If commit succeeds but the response is lost, the client retries its original ID and receives the original sequence. If a worker sends an event then crashes, replay produces a duplicate event, which devices tolerate. If a gateway dies, messages are still durable and reconnect history fills the gap. If a device is slow, bound its send buffer and disconnect with a resumable cursor rather than allowing unbounded memory growth. 
 When database quorum is unavailable, do not acknowledge durable acceptance. Quorum is the required number of replicas participating in an operation under the selected replication scheme. A gateway may keep a local optimistic message marked “sending,” but must not label it committed. For blocked or removed members, recheck membership before history reads and sends; transport connection authentication from ten minutes ago is insufficient. Rate limits and spam controls should apply per sender and conversation, with explicit rejection rather than silently dropped accepted messages. 
 Alternatives, cost, and evolution  Reject “use WebSockets and Redis Pub/Sub” as a complete design: transient delivery alone cannot recover offline history. Reject global sequence allocation because unrelated conversations do not require shared ordering. Client-generated timestamps are useful metadata but unsuitable as the sole ordering authority. A single SQL store may be sufficient at this assumed write rate; partition based on measured storage and query pressure, not messaging fashion. 
 For multi-region service, start with one home region per conversation and route writes there. Regional failover needs a fencing epoch, a version proving which owner is allowed to write, plus a documented recovery point and replay strategy. Active writers in two regions cannot casually promise one strict sequence during a partition. Encryption key custody, user export/deletion, moderation access, and audit retention require product decisions before claiming end-to-end encryption. 
 Track acceptance latency and error rate, oldest undelivered event, reconnect gap recovery, gateway connection count, buffer pressure, and deduplication rate. Test deleting a gateway mid-send and losing a response after commit. Sample content-free traces using message IDs and protect metadata because communication patterns can themselves be sensitive. 
 Follow-ups and rubric   Practice: can you guarantee exactly one notification and exactly one stored message?  A database uniqueness constraint can ensure one stored logical message per idempotency key. External push effects can duplicate across ambiguous retries unless the provider supports equivalent deduplication. State the boundary instead of promising universal exactly-once behavior.    Practice: a recipient comes online after seven days.  Fetch durable history from the saved sequence in bounded pages, then merge live events with deduplication. A connection registry or transient queue is not the history source.    Strong:  states acceptance semantics, handles ambiguous commit and reconnect, and distinguishes device delivery from read state.  Weak:  equates an open socket with reliability, orders by wall clocks, or loses offline messages. Principal depth includes failover fencing, abuse policy, and privacy implications of encryption choices. 
 Technical references checked 2026-10-19:  WebSocket protocol, RFC 6455 ;  PostgreSQL constraints . Durability and failover guarantees depend on the selected deployment configuration.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  Does sent mean accepted by our database or shown on the recipient device?  Interviewer:  Accepted durably by the service.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  The socket connection dies immediately after commit. Do you send a second message?  Candidate:  The client retries its stable message ID. The conversation uniqueness constraint returns the existing committed sequence. Delivery retries can repeat frames, so the recipient deduplicates by message identity and resumes from its last durable cursor. I would label delivered and read as separate states rather than misrepresenting the durable acknowledgment.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Case 4 · Reliable listing photos and video
text:
A seller uploads a bicycle video over an unreliable mobile connection. Media bytes need a separate data path from control metadata. This case trains resumability, asynchronous state machines, authorization, and cost reasoning. 
 Exact interview prompt  Design photo and short-video uploads for Corner Market. Uploads must resume after network interruption, files must be checked before publication, and popular listings should load quickly. 
 Clarifications and assumed requirements  Ask maximum size, formats, privacy, processing needs, and freshness. Assume 100,000 uploads/day, average original size 20 MB, maximum 500 MB, public listing media after validation, and one original plus resized/transcoded outputs. Do not make private chat attachments publicly accessible by reusing this policy. Upload completion can precede readiness; processing p95 under two minutes for supported files is a proposed target requiring benchmarking. Metadata API availability objective is 99.9% monthly. A successful upload means durable original bytes verified by the service; “ready” additionally means checks and transformations succeeded. 
 Use decimal MB and GB. Average ingress is 100,000 × 20 MB = 2 TB/day, or about 23.15 MB/s; assumed 10× peak is 231.5 MB/s before overhead. At 30 days original retention, originals total 60 TB. Assume all generated outputs add 50% of original bytes: 1 TB/day and 30 TB retained, giving 90 TB logical media storage before replicas and versioning. If each upload generates 50 views and each view transfers an assumed 1 MB, delivery is 5 TB/day. Transfer and transcoding can dominate metadata cost. 
 Contract and data model   POST /v1/uploads { filename, declared_size, media_type, checksum }
→ { upload_id, expires_at, part_size, signed_part_urls }
POST /v1/uploads/{id}/complete { parts: [{ number, checksum, token }] }
→ 202 { state: "verifying" }
GET /v1/uploads/{id} → { state, reason_code, ready_variants }
DELETE /v1/uploads/{id} → cancellation request

uploads(id PRIMARY KEY, owner_id, storage_key UNIQUE,
        declared_size, actual_size, checksum, state, version, expires_at)
variants(upload_id, kind, object_key, checksum,
         UNIQUE(upload_id, kind))
processing_jobs(upload_id, pipeline_version, state, attempt,
                UNIQUE(upload_id, pipeline_version))  
 A signed upload URL grants time-limited permission for a specific storage operation. It is a bearer capability: whoever holds it can exercise its permission. Do not put it in analytics logs. An unpredictable object key and restricted creator permissions reduce exposure but do not replace ownership checks in the control API. 
 Labeled data and control paths  CONTROL: Seller → upload API/auth → upload metadata database
                                  → short-lived scoped upload URLs
BYTES:   Seller ── multipart data ─→ private quarantine object storage
COMPLETE: API → verify object/parts → state + durable processing event
PROCESS: queue → isolated scanner/decoder → resize/transcode workers
                         ↓ failure             ↓ success
                      rejected             publish ready variants
READ:    Viewer → content delivery network → ready object storage 
 Progressive design  Start with a single object upload for small images and a metadata row. Keep originals in a private quarantine location. Add multipart upload for large or unreliable transfers: divide the object into separately retryable parts, then complete assembly. With a 10 MB chosen part size, a 500 MB object has 50 parts. A failure on part 49 need not resend the preceding 480 MB. Keep concurrency bounded so one upload does not overwhelm mobile bandwidth or create excessive requests. 
 The API allocates the storage key, records owner, expected size, checksum, and expiry, then signs only necessary operations. On completion, verify actual stored size, checksum semantics, upload ownership, and all expected parts. An object-storage ETag is not universally a whole-file cryptographic checksum, particularly for multipart objects; use an explicitly supported checksum mechanism. Server verification must not trust a client's declaration that a file is an image. 
 Use a state machine: initiated → uploading → verifying → processing → ready, with rejected, expired, and cancelled terminal states. A state machine explicitly defines allowed transitions. Apply conditional updates using a version so a late worker cannot publish a cancelled upload. Repeated completion returns the current state. A persistent outbox or reconciler closes the gap between marking verified and scheduling processing; database and object storage do not share one ordinary transaction. 
 Processing and delivery deep dives  Workers identify actual formats, enforce decoded pixel/frame/duration limits, scan as appropriate, and run parsers in resource-limited isolated environments. A small compressed file can expand into enormous memory. Never execute uploaded content or trust filenames. Produce immutable output keys incorporating upload ID and pipeline version. Retrying a job can safely overwrite only its own deterministic unpublished output or detect an already verified output; publication is a conditional metadata transition. 
 A content delivery network (CDN) caches objects near viewers. Use immutable versioned paths and long cache lifetimes for public ready variants. Deleting metadata alone does not purge a CDN, so define takedown propagation and purge operations. For restricted media, use an authenticated delivery mechanism with bounded signed access lifetimes and explicit cache rules. Do not assume the listing page's login protects a publicly addressable object. 
 Failure analysis  If a client disappears, a lifecycle rule or sweeper aborts abandoned multipart uploads and expires metadata after a documented window. Otherwise uploaded parts can accumulate cost indefinitely. If completion succeeds but its response is lost, retry queries current state; do not allocate a second object. If the worker queue is delayed, show processing status and backlog age rather than publishing unchecked bytes. If a worker crashes after writing output but before state transition, retry validates existing output and completes the transition. 
 If the metadata database fails after object creation, reconciliation finds orphan objects using a bounded inventory process and deletes only after a grace period. If storage emits duplicate or out-of-order notifications, deduplicate by upload and pipeline version, and verify current state before processing. Notifications are hints to inspect durable state, not proof of readiness. Cancellation and publication must contend through the same conditional transition to prevent a race. 
 Alternatives and evolution  Proxying every byte through the application server simplifies a tiny prototype but ties API scaling to bandwidth and long-lived requests. Direct-to-storage uploads avoid that bottleneck while requiring careful capability scoping. Reject synchronous scanning in the upload request for large videos because processing time and retries exceed ordinary request budgets. Reject storing media blobs in the primary relational database for this workload unless an unusual transactional requirement outweighs backup and serving costs. 
 Monitor completion rate by device/network, orphan bytes, incomplete upload age, scanner failures, processing backlog age, cost per ready minute of video, CDN hit ratio, and origin traffic. Avoid auto-scaling solely on queue length: a 500 MB video costs more than a small image; measure work units and memory pressure. Add adaptive video formats only after device support and viewing behavior justify them. Regional upload acceleration is a latency/cost choice to benchmark, not a default requirement. 
 Follow-ups and rubric   Practice: an upload URL leaks before expiry. Can you call it single use?  Not by default. The exact storage capability may be reusable while valid. Use short expiry, narrowly scoped keys and permissions, controlled finalization, and explicit provider-supported conditional mechanisms where required. Do not promise revocation that the chosen capability cannot enforce.    Practice: moderation rejects an already popular published file.  Set authoritative status to removed, stop issuing access, purge caches, remove ready references, and record purge completion against the takedown objective. Existing downloaded copies cannot be recalled.    Strong:  separates accepted bytes from ready media, designs idempotent state transitions, verifies content, and budgets orphan/egress cost.  Weak:  treats a client completion call or storage event as proof of safety, publishes originals immediately, or assumes a signed URL is single use. Principal depth includes parser isolation, reconciliation ownership, and takedown guarantees. 
 Technical references checked 2026-10-19:  S3 multipart upload ;  S3 signed URL behavior . AWS is a concrete example; verify limits and checksum behavior for the chosen storage provider.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  Can an upload be visible before validation completes?  Interviewer:  No; only verified and scanned media may be published.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  The object exists but finalize timed out. Should the client upload it again?  Candidate:  First retry finalize with the existing upload ID. The service checks object identity, size and checksum and conditionally advances metadata. A stored object alone is not publication authority. Cleanup uses an age threshold and state check so it does not erase an active upload; validation workers remain idempotent.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Case 5 · Find the right bicycle
text:
Residents want “blue bicycle under 200 nearby,” not every row containing those letters. Search separates transactional truth, a derived retrieval index, and relevance quality. A fast result that exposes a removed listing is still wrong. 
 Exact interview prompt  Design listing search for Corner Market with text, category, price, and distance filters. New listings should appear quickly. Explain indexing, pagination, relevance, and behavior when the search cluster fails. 
 Clarifications and assumptions  Assume 10 million active public listings, 1 million new or updated listings/day, and 10 million searches/day. Text is short titles and descriptions; no web crawling. Include exact category/price filters and geographic radius; defer semantic vector search until evidence shows a need. Ask how sold or private listings behave: authoritative eligibility must be checked before display and again before reservation. New listings should become searchable within 30 seconds at p95; removed listings must stop appearing within five seconds under healthy dependencies. If the authoritative eligibility check is unavailable, suppress uncertain results. 
 Propose 99.9% monthly search availability and server-side p95 latency under 300 ms. These are negotiated targets, not inherent engine properties. Search freshness is separate from write success: the listing creation response confirms database commit, with a “search indexing pending” state if necessary. Do not promise immediate search visibility from a successful database write. 
 Calculate workload  10 million searches/day / 86,400 ≈ 115.7 queries/s average, and 1,157/s at assumed 10× peak. Updates average 11.6/s and peak at 116/s under the same factor. At an assumed 2 KB searchable document, raw document content is 20 GB; an assumed 3× indexing expansion gives 60 GB for one complete index copy. One replica doubles this to 120 GB, before spare capacity and segment merge overhead. A full blue-green rebuild temporarily needs both old and new index generations: at least 240 GB under these simplifying assumptions. 
 If a worker indexes an assumed measured 1,000 documents/s, rebuilding 10 million documents requires 10,000 seconds, about 2.78 hours before catch-up and verification. The number is an explicit planning assumption. Benchmark real mappings and analyzers: token count, field cardinality, and update frequency affect storage and throughput substantially. 
 API, data model, and diagram   GET /v1/search?q=blue+bicycle&category=bikes&max_price_minor=20000
    &currency=USD&lat=...&lon=...&radius_m=5000&cursor=...
→ { results, next_cursor, index_freshness_seconds, degraded }

listings(id PRIMARY KEY, seller_id, title, description,
         price_minor, currency, category, location, status, version)
outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, listing_id, listing_version, operation)
search_document(id, version, analyzed_title, analyzed_description,
                price_minor, currency, category, geo_point, status)  
 WRITE: Listing API → transaction: listings + outbox
                                           ↓ dispatcher
                                      durable change stream
                                           ↓ version-aware indexer
                                      search index generation
QUERY: Browser → search API → retrieval/ranking → candidate IDs
                          → batch authoritative eligibility check
                          → bounded hydration → results
REBUILD: database snapshot + change watermark → new generation → alias switch 
 Progressive design  For an early product, a relational database with proper text search and indexes can satisfy modest scale with fewer moving parts. Once retrieval features, query load, or ranking experimentation justify separation, add a search index as a rebuildable derived view. A derived view stores data computed from an authoritative source. It is not the transaction system for inventory or payment decisions. 
 An inverted index maps a normalized term to the documents containing it. An analyzer transforms text into terms through tokenization and optional normalization. Test how “bikes,” “bike,” punctuation, and multiple languages behave; blindly stemming product model names can damage precision. Precision measures how many retrieved results are relevant; recall measures how much relevant material was retrieved. Neither equals service latency. 
 The listing transaction writes an outbox event with a monotonically increasing listing version. A dispatcher retries delivery; the indexer ignores older versions so delayed updates cannot overwrite new content. Represent deletions as versioned tombstones and retain them long enough to cover possible replay. A fresh index rebuild must also honor changes after its snapshot watermark. Otherwise a deleted listing can reappear after cutover. 
 Retrieval, ranking, and pagination  Apply structured price, currency, category, status, and distance constraints as filters. Rank remaining candidates using text relevance plus carefully bounded product signals such as recency or distance. State where ranking is applied: candidate retrieval followed by optional reranking of a bounded set. A reranker cannot recover relevant items excluded by retrieval. Use minimum query length, bounded radius, bounded page size, and timeouts to limit expensive queries and abuse. 
 For stable pagination, return an opaque cursor containing the sort tuple and a bounded search-session or point-in-time identifier if the engine supports it. A point-in-time view fixes the index state for a search session; it consumes resources and expires. Use a deterministic ID tie-breaker after relevance score. Explain expired cursors explicitly and restart the query. Deep numeric offsets require work over discarded results and shift under updates; avoid offering unlimited page numbers. 
 Hydrate candidates in one bounded batch instead of one database call per hit. Recheck current public/sold/deleted eligibility and authorization against a reliable source or a tightly controlled revocation mechanism. Oversample to fill a page after filtering, but cap rounds and total candidates. A total-hit count from a stale search view can differ from currently displayable listings; label it approximate or omit it. 
 Failure and correctness analysis  If indexing stalls, keep accepting listing writes while exposing freshness and alerting on oldest unprocessed event age. If the search cluster fails, return a deliberately limited recent/category browse view if the database has capacity; do not silently run unbounded wildcard SQL across 10 million rows. Protect fallback with concurrency limits and its own latency budget. Search availability may be lower than listing-write availability; that is an explicit product tradeoff. 
 If a shard is unavailable, decide whether partial results are acceptable and mark them. A shard is one partition of the index. Replicas improve read availability but a correlated deployment or zone failure can still affect both if placement is poor. During a hot query surge, cache public query results with bounded freshness and eligibility filtering. Do not put precise personal locations in shared cache keys or broad logs unnecessarily. 
 Alternatives, operations, and evolution  Reject treating the search index as the sole source of sold status: indexing lag violates reservation correctness. Reject adding embeddings by default; measure failed queries, relevance, language needs, latency, and cost first. If semantic retrieval is added, combine its candidates with lexical retrieval, evaluate with judged queries, and preserve exact filters. A plausible synonym can be wrong for a specific spare part. 
 Monitor query p95/p99, error rate, zero-result rate, index lag, eligibility filtering rate, rejected expensive queries, shard size skew, and rebuild duration. Evaluate relevance with a versioned set of representative judged queries, including rare and multilingual terms. A/B experiments need guardrails for irrelevant results, seller fairness, and latency. Rebuild using snapshot plus replay, compare counts and sampled documents, shadow representative queries, then switch an alias atomically with a rollback plan. Avoid changing database schema and index generation in an incompatible single step. 
 Follow-ups and rubric   Practice: version 12 arrives before version 11, then a delete at 13. What should remain?  Accept 12, ignore 11, then record the deletion at 13. Replaying 12 must not resurrect the document. Tombstone retention and rebuild watermarks must cover the supported replay window.    Practice: the index says a bicycle is available. Can checkout reserve it?  No. Search supplies candidates. The reservation service checks authoritative current inventory and commits the reservation transaction; the result page is not a lock.    Strong:  explains derivation and replay, separates relevance from correctness, and makes filtering and rebuild cutover concrete.  Weak:  names Elasticsearch without update semantics, claims indexes are immediately current, or uses search as inventory truth. Principal depth includes relevance evaluation, migration rollback, fallback budgets, and privacy-aware observability. 
 Technical references checked 2026-10-19:  Elastic near-real-time search ;  PostgreSQL full text search . Refresh timing and engine-specific point-in-time APIs must be verified for the deployed version; our 30-second freshness objective is an application requirement.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  May results lag price and stock updates?  Interviewer:  Yes, but checkout must validate current price and inventory.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  Why not query the search index when reserving stock?  Candidate:  It is a derived view and may lag or replay out of order. I use it for candidate retrieval, then the authoritative order transaction validates the quote and available units. If search fails, a narrow database-backed catalog fallback may be acceptable, but it cannot silently promise the same ranking or throughput.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Protect the market: distributed rate limiting
text:
Worked interview • correctness boundary • 45 minutes 
 Prompt and scope   Exact prompt:  “Design a distributed rate limiter for Corner Market. Protect product browsing, merchant writes, and checkout from accidental overload and abusive clients. Explain what happens when the limiter itself fails.” A rate limiter decides whether an operation may proceed within a configured traffic budget. It does not prove that a client is trustworthy, prevent every denial-of-service attack, or reserve inventory. 
 Ask before drawing   What identity is limited? Assume authenticated account plus route class, with a separate coarse anonymous network limit. Shared network addresses must not be the sole identity for logged-in shoppers.  What policy? Assume browsing allows 10 requests/second with a burst of 20, merchant mutation allows 2/second with a burst of 5. Checkout has a separate admission budget and transaction safeguards.  How strict? Assume small temporary over-admission is acceptable for browsing, but a merchant's contracted quota must not increase merely because servers are added.  Where? One region initially; three regions later. Global billing quotas are a separate durable accounting problem.  
 Goals and estimates  Assume 100,000 daily active shoppers, 200 API requests per active shopper per day, and a peak ten times the daily average. These are interview inputs, not observed production measurements. Traffic is 20,000,000 / 86,400 = 231.48 requests/second on average; use 2,315 requests/second for peak planning. Assume 50,000 concurrently active identity/route keys. At a planning allowance of 200 bytes per key including overhead, state is about 10 MB per copy; measure the actual datastore representation before buying capacity. One atomic decision per request creates about 2,315 datastore operations/second at peak. A tenfold safety scenario is 23,150 decisions/second, not a claim that one node can sustain it.  The proposed service-level objective (SLO), a measurable reliability target, is 99.9% successful limiter decisions monthly with added latency below 5 milliseconds at the 99th percentile inside the region. A percentile says what fraction of observations finish below a threshold. Set an explicit timeout smaller than the caller's remaining deadline. Rejections should be distinguishable from dependency failures, and policy changes should become visible within one minute. 
 Interface, state, and diagram   Check(subject, route_class, cost=1, policy_version)
  → {allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms, reason}
HTTP rejection: 429 Too Many Requests; Retry-After in seconds
bucket key: (tenant_id, subject_hash, route_class, policy_version)
value: {tokens_scaled_integer, last_refill_ms}
policy: {rate_per_second, capacity, expires_at}   Never accept tenant identity or the policy version directly from an untrusted header. Authenticate at the gateway and derive the key there. Hashing an identifier reduces accidental exposure but does not automatically make the data anonymous. Keep raw identities out of metrics labels.  [Client]
   | HTTPS request
   v
[Gateway: authenticate + classify route]
   | bounded Check RPC
   v
[Limiter instances] ---- policy refresh ---- [Versioned policy store]
   | atomic bucket update
   v
[Sharded bucket store: one owner per key]
   |
   +-- allowed --> [Market API]
   +-- denied  --> [429 + retry guidance] 
 Build the smallest correct design  Start with one process and a token bucket. A token represents permission for one unit of work; the bucket refills at rate  r  up to capacity  B . For elapsed seconds  dt , compute  available = min(B, old_tokens + r × dt) . Admit only if available covers cost, then subtract cost. This bounds accepted work over any interval of length  t  by roughly  B + r × t , assuming a correct monotonic elapsed-time calculation. A full browsing bucket admits 20 immediate requests. Request 21 needs 0.1 seconds of refill at 10 tokens/second.  Two gateways independently storing a full bucket would admit 40 immediate requests. Move each identity's state to a shared owner and combine read, refill, decision, and write into one atomic operation: other requests cannot observe a half-completed update. A short Redis script is one implementation option; atomic script execution does not imply durable global consensus. Use integer-scaled tokens to make rounding explicit, clamp negative elapsed time to zero, and cap large elapsed intervals at a full bucket. Prefer time obtained consistently at the state owner; wall-clock jumps still require a documented policy and tests.  Expire idle bucket state only after enough idle time to refill completely. Deleting a partially empty bucket early grants a fresh burst. Include policy version in the key only with a deliberate migration rule: changing versions resets state and can grant another burst. An alternative updates rate and capacity while preserving and clamping existing tokens. Test rollout behavior, not merely steady state. 
 Deep dives: contention and geography  Hash identity keys across partitions. A hot merchant remains one hot key even after adding partitions. Local token leases can amortize calls: a central owner grants a gateway a bounded number of tokens, which it spends locally. Define the extra admitted work during a failure as at most the total unspent outstanding leases, provided leases cannot be reused after reassignment. Give leases expiry and an owner generation. This spends accuracy to gain availability and latency; do not describe it as exact.  For three regions, choose a home region for strict per-account policy, accepting remote latency and reduced availability during partitions. For browsing, split a global budget into regional allocations whose sum is bounded and rebalance conservatively. Three regions each enforcing the entire nominal global budget triples the allowance. An exact global decision across a partition cannot simultaneously offer uninterrupted independent regional admission; state the business choice rather than hiding it behind a product name. 
 Failure analysis and alternatives  If the bucket store times out, browsing may use a deliberately smaller local emergency budget, with a metric identifying degraded decisions. This is bounded fail-open behavior: some requests continue without the normal shared decision. Merchant writes can fail closed with a retriable dependency error, subject to the product's tolerance for lost availability. Neither policy should bypass authentication, authorization, or payment correctness. A retry after an uncertain decision might consume two tokens; conservative double charging is acceptable here, but must not become a duplicate checkout charge.  Reject a fixed one-minute counter when smooth overload control matters: 100 requests at the end of one minute and 100 at the start of the next may pass almost together. A sliding log records every timestamp and offers a precise rolling window but consumes memory proportional to request volume. A sliding counter is a cheaper approximation. Token buckets fit our explicit burst contract; they do not offer a strict “no more than N in every rolling minute” promise.  Track allowed and denied counts, decision latency, store failures, hot partitions, policy age, and emergency mode usage. Alert on saturation and unexpected admission changes, not on every rejection. Set per-tenant fairness and weighted costs so a cheap metadata lookup and expensive export do not share a misleading one-request cost. Protect the limiter's own API and cap key cardinality to prevent attackers manufacturing endless keys. 
 Evolution and interview close  Begin with a shared regional state owner plus measured failover behavior. Add partitions after measuring load, leases only after quantifying accuracy tolerance, and regional allocation only when geography requires it. Cost includes one decision per call, replication, policy distribution, and operational complexity. Test two concurrent requests for the final token, clock rollback, policy transition, failover with lost recent state, and a single identity producing most traffic.   Practice: a gateway holds a lease of 8 tokens and crashes. What is the safe interpretation?  The central owner already deducted those 8 tokens. Losing unused tokens temporarily under-admits. Reissuing them before proving they cannot still be spent risks over-admission. A restarted gateway must not reuse an old lease generation.    Interviewer follow-ups and answer rubric   Follow-ups:  How does a premium tenant get weighted service? Can a successful retry be charged twice? What exact bound is relaxed during regional failure?  Strong:  names the quota identity, derives burst behavior, makes state transition atomic, and quantifies degraded admission.  Weak:  says “put Redis at the gateway,” counts separately on every server, or promises exact global quotas and full partition availability without explaining coordination.   Technical reference checked 2026-10-19:  Redis scripting documentation  confirms scripts execute atomically and block other server activity while running; keep scripts bounded. All sizing, policies, and architecture choices above are fictional design assumptions.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  Is the limit a strict global entitlement or regional abuse protection?  Interviewer:  Begin with regional abuse protection.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  Can we simply deploy the same bucket in three regions?  Candidate:  Only if the contract permits the multiplied allowance. For a strict global budget I would allocate bounded regional rights or coordinate through one owner; the former can strand capacity and the latter adds latency and partition unavailability. I would keep billing quotas in a separate durable accounting path.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Run it later: a durable job scheduler
text:
Worked interview • leases and duplicate effects • 45 minutes 
 Prompt and clarifications   Exact prompt:  “Design a durable scheduler for Corner Market. Merchants schedule sale reminders and nightly inventory reports. Jobs must survive crashes, run close to their requested time, retry safely, and support cancellation.” Durable means acknowledged work remains recoverable after the failures covered by the storage contract. Scheduling decides when work becomes eligible; workers perform the actual effects.   One-time or recurring? Assume both. Recurrence uses an explicit named timezone and a defined daylight-saving policy; store each generated occurrence separately.  Timing precision? Assume 99% of eligible jobs start within 30 seconds when dependencies are healthy. This is a start-delay target, not a completion promise.  Delivery semantics? Assume jobs may execute more than once. The observable business effect should be deduplicated where possible.  Cancellation? Define “start” as the successful atomic claim transition into RUNNING. Cancellation that wins before that claim prevents execution; after the claim it is best effort, even if the worker has not yet called the external provider. An email already accepted by an external provider may be impossible to recall.  
 Numbers that drive choices  Assume 1,000,000 jobs/day, an average runtime of 2 seconds, and a peak arrival rate ten times average. Average rate is 1,000,000 / 86,400 = 11.57 jobs/second; round peak to 116 jobs/second. Little's Law relates average work in progress to throughput times duration in a stable system: at peak, 116 × 2 = 232 concurrent executions. At a planning utilization of 70%, need about 232 / 0.7 = 332 execution slots. Slots are concurrency capacity, not necessarily machines; CPU-heavy and waiting-heavy jobs require different sizing.  At 1 KB of metadata per job and 30 days of retained history, 30 million rows require about 30 GB of raw metadata, before indexes and replication. Large report payloads belong in object storage with references in the job record. If all one million jobs arrive at midnight, the tenfold peak assumption is false: identify scheduled bursts, introduce allowed jitter, and provision or negotiate the completion window.  Other goals: no acknowledged job silently disappears after a single worker failure, tenant isolation, bounded retries, auditable state changes, and a clearly documented disaster recovery point. Recovery point objective is the acceptable amount of recent data loss; recovery time objective is the acceptable restoration duration. Neither follows automatically from “database replication.” 
 API, state, and architecture   POST /jobs  Idempotency-Key: merchant-scoped-key
{type, payload_ref, run_at_utc, deadline_utc, tenant_id}
GET /jobs/{job_id}
POST /jobs/{job_id}/cancel
jobs(id, tenant_id, type, payload_ref, run_at, state,
     attempt, lease_until, lease_generation, idempotency_key,
     request_hash, last_error, created_at)
UNIQUE(tenant_id, idempotency_key)
INDEX(state, run_at, id)
job_events(job_id, sequence, state, reason, occurred_at)   Idempotency means repeating the same logical request has the same intended effect. Reuse of a key with a different request body returns a conflict instead of silently changing the job. Authenticate ownership before reads and cancellations. Permit only registered job types and validated parameters; arbitrary uploaded code is a different, much harder isolation problem.  [Merchant] -- create/cancel --> [Job API]
                                  |
                                  v
                          [Durable job database]
                                  ^
                                  | claim due rows + lease
                          [Worker pool per job class]
                                  |
                      idempotent business operation
                                  v
                      [Report store / delivery provider]

[Lease reaper] --> expired running jobs --> retry eligibility
[Recurrence expander] --> uniquely keyed future occurrences 
 Progressive design: transaction first  Start with a database-backed queue. Workers select due pending rows inside a short transaction, acquire row locks, and update them to running with a lease. A lease grants temporary ownership until a timestamp. With PostgreSQL,  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED  lets competing workers skip already locked rows; its inconsistent view is suitable for queue-like selection, not general reporting. Commit the claim before doing slow external work. Holding database locks while generating a report or calling an email service ties storage availability to slow dependencies.  Each claim increments  lease_generation . Completion is conditional on matching job ID, running state, and generation. A stale worker whose lease expired cannot overwrite a newer worker's result. This generation is a fencing token, a monotonically increasing ownership marker. It fences database state; an external effect also needs its own deduplication or fencing support. Heartbeats extend leases with the same generation. Pick a lease longer than normal execution and renew well before expiry, while accepting that pauses and network partitions can still cause overlapping workers.  Poll due work every second with a bounded batch. Use the database clock consistently for due and lease comparisons. Add randomized poll delays and an index so idle workers do not repeatedly scan history. Separate short notifications from long reports, and enforce tenant concurrency limits so one merchant cannot occupy every slot. A broker can later transport ready jobs, but the database remains the authority for scheduled eligibility; publishing must then use a transactional outbox to avoid losing jobs between commit and send. 
 The unavoidable duplicate window  Consider a worker that sends a reminder successfully and crashes before marking the job completed. The lease expires and another worker retries. Marking complete before sending instead creates a lost-effect window. A scheduler alone cannot make an arbitrary external side effect happen exactly once. Pass the stable occurrence ID as the downstream idempotency key when the provider supports a documented durable deduplication contract. Otherwise record the uncertainty and choose explicitly between possible duplicates and possible omission.  For reports, write output under a stable job-derived object key and publish a manifest conditionally. For internal database work, insert the business effect and mark completion in the same transaction when both share a database. A unique constraint on effect ID is the final concurrency defense. Retain deduplication records long enough to cover retries, replays, and backup restoration; a five-minute record is insufficient if operators can replay a month later. 
 Retries, cancellation, and failure  Classify permanent validation errors separately from temporary timeouts. Retry temporary failures with exponential backoff and random jitter, cap both attempts and elapsed time, and stop after the job deadline. A dead-letter state preserves exhausted work for inspection; it is not an unmonitored trash folder. Alert on oldest eligible age, failure rate by class, lease expiry, and queue depth. Compare incoming work with sustainable completion rate: if arrival exceeds processing, no retry policy can prevent backlog growth.  Cancellation uses a conditional update. Pending becomes cancelled; running becomes cancel_requested, and the worker checks between safe steps. Cancellation and completion racing must have an explicitly allowed outcome. Recurring schedules need a stable occurrence key such as schedule ID plus intended UTC instant, a timezone database version or documented update policy, and a choice for missed runs after outages: catch up all, latest only, or skip. Never “just add 24 hours” to model every local calendar day.  Database failover can repeat claims if recent writes were lost. Ensure the promised recovery point matches business expectations, keep effects idempotent, and test restoration. A worker that loses connectivity must stop starting new effects once it cannot renew ownership; a paused process resuming later still requires fencing. Large outages may create retry storms, so recover gradually with global and tenant admission controls. 
 Alternatives, evolution, and assessment  Reject an in-memory timer on an API server: restarts erase it, replicas disagree, and deployments shift responsibility. Reject a single cron entry per job at this scale: mutation, cancellation, observability, and ownership become fragile. Begin with indexed due rows; shard by tenant or due-time bucket only when measured lock contention or storage demands it. Partition old history for retention and benchmark due-row queries at realistic backlog sizes. Cost follows retained metadata, polling frequency, execution duration, and repeated work.   Practice: the job takes 90 seconds but its lease is 30 seconds. Diagnose and redesign.  Without renewal, another worker can start at 30 seconds. Renew the lease conditionally, measure heartbeat health, and retain generation checks. This reduces overlaps but does not eliminate them; make effects idempotent. For a non-idempotent external operation, reconcile its status after an uncertain response rather than blindly retrying.    Interviewer follow-ups and rubric   Follow-ups:  What happens after a week-long outage? How do you stop a noisy tenant? Can an operator replay a succeeded job?  Strong:  separates start from completion, calculates concurrency, explains the duplicate window, and shows conditional ownership transitions.  Weak:  promises exactly-once email, holds locks through network calls, or treats a queue as a complete recurring scheduler.   Technical reference checked 2026-10-19:  PostgreSQL SELECT and locking documentation  describes SKIP LOCKED and its queue-oriented use. The selected architecture and all workload numbers are exercise assumptions.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  Does no duplicate job mean one accepted owner or one external side effect?  Interviewer:  The business wants one reminder email.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  A paused worker wakes after its lease expires. Are we safe?  Candidate:  The new epoch fences state writes only where the receiver checks it. For email I need provider idempotency on a stable effect ID or must disclose the duplicate-versus-loss tradeoff after an unknown result. I cannot promise one email merely because the queue has one current owner.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: The last basket: inventory, reservations, and payments
text:
Worked interview • business invariants • 50 minutes 
 Exact prompt and business contract   Exact prompt:  “Corner Market sells limited bakery pickup boxes. Design reservation and checkout so two shoppers cannot buy the last box, retries do not duplicate a charge, and payment failures do not strand inventory forever.” The central invariant, a rule that must always hold, is that confirmed plus active reserved units never exceed sellable inventory for a stock item. Payment correctness is a second invariant: one order must not accumulate multiple unintended successful charges.   Assume each checkout contains stock from one merchant; cross-merchant carts are out of scope for the first version.  Assume a reservation lasts five minutes, but payment attempts started before expiry need explicit reconciliation before stock is released.  Assume the payment provider supports idempotency keys and status lookup. Its precise key retention and webhook behavior must be checked before implementation.  Assume authorization holds funds and capture requests settlement; availability and timing depend on the chosen provider and payment method. We do not build a card network or store card credentials.  
 Scale and nonfunctional goals  Assume 100,000 daily shoppers and 0.2 checkout attempts per shopper/day: 20,000 attempts/day, or 0.2315/second average. A 100-fold promotion peak gives 23.15 attempts/second overall. This modest aggregate does not remove contention: 2,000 simultaneous requests may target the same final 100 boxes. Model hot-item contention separately from average throughput.  Assume five minutes of active reservations at 23.15/second during a sustained peak: approximately 6,945 active reservations. At 1 KB per reservation, raw active records are roughly 6.95 MB. Twenty thousand orders/day at 2 KB each produce 40 MB/day before indexes, events, and replicas. Transaction contention and correctness dominate this exercise more than storage volume.  Target reservation responses below 300 milliseconds at the 99th percentile in-region, excluding the external payment interaction. Set a proposed 99.9% monthly reservation availability target, but never silently oversell to meet it. During an inventory partition, decline or defer affected reservations. A charge can remain pending when the outcome is unknown; showing “failed” prematurely encourages harmful retries. Maintain an auditable state history and keep sensitive payment data with the provider. 
 Model and interfaces   POST /reservations  Idempotency-Key: customer-scoped-key
{merchant_id, items:[{sku, quantity}]}
→ {reservation_id, expires_at, total_minor_units, currency}
POST /orders/{id}/pay  Idempotency-Key: payment-attempt-key

outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, aggregate_id, type, payload, sent_at)   Use integer minor currency units and a currency code; do not calculate money with binary floating point. Obtain prices from trusted server state and store the quoted order amount. Define rounding and tax rules separately. Create or lock the scoped request record in the same transaction as the reservation/order effect. A concurrent identical key waits for the durable result or receives an explicit in-progress response. Lock the order before creating a payment attempt, and enforce at most one live attempt per order (for example a partial unique index over order_id for pending/unknown attempts). A different client key must not bypass that order invariant. Reconcile an unknown attempt before permitting another charge attempt. A request hash prevents one idempotency key being reused with different items. A uniqueness constraint is enforced in storage, not by an earlier “does this exist?” query that races.
