 Progressive design: keep stock atomic  Begin with one transactional database for a merchant's inventory and orders. A transaction updates stock only if  sellable - reserved - sold >= requested_quantity , then inserts the reservation and order. Check affected row count. For several stock items, lock rows in a deterministic SKU order, verify all quantities, and commit all or none. Consistent locking order reduces deadlocks; the application must still retry a deadlock-aborted transaction safely. Do not read availability, release the connection, and later subtract: both buyers could read one remaining unit.  For 100 boxes, reserving 3 sets reserved to 3 and leaves 97 available. Confirmation moves 3 from reserved to sold in one transaction; availability stays 97. Expiry moves 3 out of reserved and leaves sold unchanged. Every transition checks the current reservation state. Expiring twice cannot release 6 units. A cache may show approximate availability for browsing, but the transactional conditional update decides whether checkout succeeds.  A durable state machine makes permitted transitions explicit: HELD → PAYMENT_PENDING → CONFIRMED, or HELD → EXPIRED; PAYMENT_PENDING may become CANCELLED only after the payment outcome is resolved. Persist an attempt before calling the provider. Use its stable key for retries of that same attempt. If the response is lost, query or reconcile the original attempt instead of creating a new key and another possible charge. 
 Where a transaction stops  The inventory database and external provider do not share our local transaction. Use a saga, a sequence of durable steps with compensating actions when later steps cannot complete. Authorize funds, atomically confirm stock and order if the reservation is still eligible, then capture according to the business contract. If stock confirmation cannot complete after authorization, void the authorization when supported. If capture happens but finalization fails, reconcile and either complete the order or refund. Refund is a new business action that may take time and fail; it does not erase the original charge.  An authorization-first workflow needs a policy for capture failure after confirmation: retain the order in a recoverable pending state, retry within a bounded window, then cancel and release or return stock according to merchant policy. Reserving inventory during payment uncertainty reduces immediate availability but avoids selling the same box to someone else. Describe this tradeoff to the interviewer; there is no magic ordering that eliminates all external uncertainty.  Insert order events into an outbox in the same transaction as the business transition. A publisher sends unsent events and may send twice after a crash; consumers deduplicate using event ID. Publishing directly before commit creates phantom events, while publishing only afterward without durable intent can lose events. Webhooks can also be duplicated or arrive out of order. Authenticate provider signatures, deduplicate provider event IDs, and reconcile against permitted state transitions and authoritative provider status rather than trusting arrival order. 
 Failures, alternatives, and operating model  An expiry worker conditionally expires only eligible held reservations. It cannot blindly release PAYMENT_PENDING stock at five minutes: a charge might have succeeded during a timeout. Track an uncertainty deadline, look up provider status, and escalate stuck cases with operational visibility. Use the database's time for expiry comparisons. Test the exact boundary where expiry and confirmation race, plus crash-after-provider-success and duplicate-webhook sequences.  Reject a cache lock as the sole overselling defense: lease expiry can let another process enter while the first still runs. Reject separate inventory writes followed by order writes without a transaction or documented compensation. Reject a blanket claim of “exactly-once payments”; the relevant guarantee is stable request identity plus provider deduplication, reconciliation, and constrained state transitions.  Track reserved-age distribution, payment-pending age, stock invariant violations, authorization-to-capture lag, reconciliation backlog, and duplicate-key conflicts. Log correlation IDs and provider references without storing secrets. Restrict refund and manual-adjustment privileges; audit operator actions. Reconcile totals against provider settlement records on a scheduled basis because callbacks alone are not a financial ledger.  Scale by merchant when merchants own disjoint stock. A single hot SKU remains serialized at its correctness boundary; shard counters only with an explicit stock-allocation scheme whose allocations sum to the actual stock. Multi-region writes should route a stock owner to one authoritative region or use an appropriate strongly coordinated store. Cross-region independent decrements cannot safely enforce one remaining unit during a partition. Evolve cross-merchant carts into per-merchant reservations with explicit partial-failure handling, rather than pretending the original single-database transaction extends globally.   Practice: the provider times out, then the shopper presses Pay again. What should the service do?  Return the existing attempt's pending status, retry or look up that attempt using its original provider key, and reconcile. Do not assume timeout means failure. If the provider's deduplication window has elapsed, investigate before issuing another charge.    Follow-ups and rubric   Follow-ups:  What if price changes during checkout? Who can adjust stock? What happens when refunds fail?  Strong:  states invariants, demonstrates conditional updates, exposes payment uncertainty, and names the recovery owner.  Weak:  reads cached stock as authoritative, uses a new key for every retry, or releases stock while payment status is unknown.   Technical reference checked 2026-10-19:  PostgreSQL row-locking documentation . Provider-specific payment guarantees are intentionally requirements to verify, rather than assumed universal behavior. All merchant and workload details are fictional.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  What should happen if payment succeeds after the hold expires?  Interviewer:  Do not oversell; refund if stock cannot be obtained safely.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  Why not roll back the SQL transaction to reverse the charge?  Candidate:  The provider is another authority. A local rollback cannot undo its committed effect. I reconcile the stable payment identity, then attempt the permitted order transition. If inventory cannot be reacquired, I create an auditable refund action with its own retry and reconciliation state, rather than calling the whole workflow atomic.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Count what happened: merchant analytics and streaming
text:
Worked interview • time, replay, and accounting boundaries • 45 minutes 
 Prompt and assumed answers   Exact prompt:  “Build Corner Market's merchant dashboard showing product views, checkout conversion, and paid order totals within one minute. Support historical reports and recovery after processing outages.” Streaming means processing a continuing sequence of events incrementally. An event is a record of something that happened, with an identity and occurrence time; it is not automatically a unique or trustworthy fact.   Is the dashboard financially authoritative? Assume view and funnel numbers are approximate operational analytics. Paid totals originate from confirmed order transitions and are reconciled against the order database. Settlement reporting is separate.  How fresh? Assume 95% of valid events become queryable within 60 seconds during healthy operation. Late events can correct recent windows for 24 hours.  How long retained? Assume 7 days in the replay log, 1 year in object storage, and 90 days of fine-grained aggregates.  Can clients resend? Yes. Client timestamps may be wrong, and mobile devices can upload later. Trust server-recorded order events more than client claims.  
 Capacity and contracts  Assume 100,000 daily shoppers, each producing 50 product-interaction events/day. That is 5,000,000 events/day, or 57.87/second average. Tenfold peak is about 579/second. At 500 bytes per encoded event, raw traffic is 2.5 GB/day, 17.5 GB for seven days, or 52.5 GB with three log copies, before protocol overhead and indexes. A year of raw events is approximately 912.5 GB before compression and redundant storage. Compression is workload-dependent; benchmark rather than claiming a universal ratio.  Assume 2,000 merchants, 20 relevant products per merchant, and two event counters per one-minute window. A dense upper bound is 2,000 × 20 × 2 × 1,440 = 115.2 million counter cells/day. Sparse activity, coarser historical windows, and retaining only useful dimensions can save far more than changing storage brands. Do not materialize every user, product, region, campaign, and device combination without a query requirement.  The proposed ingestion target is 99.9% monthly successful server acknowledgments after the configured durable log write. Define which failures that durability covers. Track ingestion latency separately from end-to-end freshness. A service can accept every event while its dashboard is hours stale. 
 Event contract and architecture   POST /events/batch
{events:[{event_id, event_type, schema_version, occurred_at,
          session_id, product_id, merchant_id}]}
server adds: received_at, authenticated_subject, validation_result
order event: {event_id, order_id, order_version,
              merchant_id, paid_minor_units, currency, occurred_at}
aggregate key: (merchant_id, product_id, window_start,
                metric_name, metric_definition_version)
GET /merchants/{id}/metrics?from=...&to=...&resolution=hour   Use an allowlist of event types, maximum batch size, schema validation, and rate limits. A schema version identifies the shape of data; a metric-definition version identifies the meaning of a computed number. They solve different problems. Server-issued merchant identity prevents one merchant writing or reading another merchant's data. Minimize personal fields and define consent, deletion, and retention requirements before collecting them.  [Web/mobile] --> [Validated ingest] --> [Partitioned durable log]
[Order database + outbox] --------------------^
                                              |
                       +----------------------+------------------+
                       v                                         v
               [Stream processor]                        [Raw object archive]
           dedupe + event-time windows                    replay / batch repair
                       |
                       v
               [Aggregate query store]  
 Start simple, then make time explicit  Begin with server-side order events written through the transactional outbox and a batch dashboard refreshed every minute. Add client views through validated ingestion. Partition the log by merchant when ordered merchant processing is useful, but recognize that one large merchant can become a hot partition. Partitioning by merchant plus a stable subkey spreads load at the cost of merging partial aggregates. Log order is normally scoped to a partition; do not assume one global ordering of every shopper's actions.  Distinguish event time, when the action occurred, from processing time, when the processor handled it. A phone records a view at 12:00 but reconnects at 12:10. Counting by processing time puts the view in the wrong minute. Count valid events into event-time windows, with a policy for implausible client timestamps. Use received time or quarantine when timestamps are outside accepted bounds, and disclose this interpretation in metric definitions.  A watermark is the processor's estimate of how far event-time progress has advanced. It is a policy informed by observations, not proof that older events can never arrive. With a two-minute lateness allowance, a window can publish a provisional value promptly, then accept updates. Our contract permits corrections for 24 hours; older arrivals go to a repair path or a separately labeled late-event count. Define what a dashboard displays when a previous total changes. 
 Duplicates, replay, and the denominator  Deduplicate by stable event ID within an explicit retention window. At 5 million events/day and 24 hours of deduplication, 32 bytes per ID is 160 MB raw before state-store overhead. A duplicated event arriving after that window can be counted again unless archival repair or a longer-lived unique record catches it. Do not sell bounded deduplication as eternal uniqueness.  Make aggregate writes replay-safe. One option writes deterministic window values keyed by window and processor version, replacing prior values rather than blindly incrementing on every delivery. Another commits processed offsets and output in a transactional boundary supported by the chosen stack. Broker-level transactional processing does not make arbitrary external databases, emails, or downstream APIs exactly once. Verify the entire boundary. During repair, write a new version of aggregates and atomically switch readers after validation instead of mixing old and new partial results.  Conversion needs a definition. “Paid orders / views” is not the same as “sessions with a paid order / sessions with a product view.” Suppose 1,000 eligible sessions contain views and 80 of those sessions pay: conversion is 80 / 1,000 = 8%. If those sessions generated 4,000 views, dividing 80 by 4,000 yields 2%, a different metric. Establish attribution window, identity rules, bot treatment, and timezone boundaries before implementing joins. Cross-device identity and missing events limit certainty; display suitable caveats. 
 Failure and operational decisions  If a processor is down for two hours while traffic averages 58/second, backlog is about 417,600 events. A recovering processor able to handle 300/second while 58/second continue arriving drains at 242/second, requiring about 1,726 seconds, or 28.8 minutes. Simply dividing by 300 understates recovery time. Provision and alert using remaining retention headroom: once seven-day log data expire, recovery needs the object archive.  Poison events must not stall an entire partition forever. Preserve failed events with reason and schema version in a quarantined stream, count them, and provide a controlled replay tool. For a query-store outage, stop or buffer within bounded capacity rather than silently advancing progress and dropping output. Track oldest unprocessed event, source-to-dashboard delay, duplicates, late-event rate, invalid events, state growth, and reconciliation differences.  Reject querying the production order database for every dashboard refresh: analytics scans can impair checkout and cannot reconstruct client views. Reject treating a cache increment as an auditable financial total. Reject starting with a complex stream platform if minute-level batch satisfies requirements. Add streaming when latency, volume, and operational ownership justify it; ongoing cost includes replicas, retained data, state checkpoints, repair jobs, and on-call expertise. 
 Evolution and practice  Keep immutable source events under retention rules, version transformations, and support deterministic backfills. If regulations require deletion, an append-only slogan does not override it: implement deletion or cryptographic and storage controls appropriate to the requirement, and propagate effects to derived data. Keep order correctness outside the analytics path so a dashboard outage cannot stop checkout.   Practice: a replay doubles paid totals. What failed, and how do you repair it?  The sink probably increments totals without deduplicating event IDs or replacing deterministic windows. Pause publication, rebuild a new aggregate version from trusted order events, compare totals to authoritative orders, and switch readers after validation. Preserve the bad run for audit without exposing it as current data.    Follow-ups and rubric   Follow-ups:  What does “one minute” measure? How do definitions change? What happens beyond retention?  Strong:  distinguishes times, derives backlog recovery, defines denominators, and bounds deduplication.  Weak:  promises exactly-once end to end from a broker setting, ignores late events, or confuses dashboard totals with settlement accounting.   Technical reference checked 2026-10-19:  Apache Kafka design documentation  explains partition ordering and the scope of transactional processing guarantees. Workload, lateness, and retention policies above are chosen interview assumptions.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  Are these dashboard counts provisional or financial settlement records?  Interviewer:  Provisional product dashboards with later corrections.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  A replay sends every event again. Will counts double?  Candidate:  Not if identity, retention and aggregate replacement are designed together. I deduplicate stable event IDs within the declared horizon and rebuild into a new version before cutover. Events older than that horizon require a separate controlled backfill. Financial settlement would need stronger source reconciliation and an explicit accounting contract.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Elective: reliable AI recommendations and feature serving
text:
Worked interview • data freshness and safe fallback • 45 minutes 
 Exact prompt and scope   Exact prompt:  “Corner Market wants personalized product recommendations. Design the feature and inference serving path, including training consistency, freshness, failure behavior, and safe rollout.” A feature is a measurable input to a model, such as a customer's seven-day category-view count. Inference is applying a trained model to inputs to obtain a prediction. This elective follows analytics because it reuses event collection, replay, and freshness reasoning; it is not a requirement to add artificial intelligence to every system.   What outcome? Assume rank up to 200 eligible candidate products and return 20. Candidate generation chooses a smaller relevant set; ranking orders that set.  What model? Assume a compact CPU-served ranking model, not a large language model. Model training research and graphics-processor infrastructure are outside this interview's scope.  What quality contract? Assume experiments evaluate useful purchases and user experience, with guardrails for errors, latency, stale inventory, and merchant concentration. No guaranteed business uplift is claimed.  Which data? Assume consented product interactions and current catalog eligibility. Never use payment credentials or sensitive personal attributes as features.  
 Capacity, latency, and freshness  Assume 100,000 daily shoppers request 20 recommendation panels/day: 2,000,000 requests/day, or 23.15 requests/second average. Tenfold peak is 232/second after rounding upward. At 200 candidates/request, peak scoring demand is 46,400 candidate scores/second. Benchmark the actual model and batch shape; this arithmetic does not determine how many CPU cores are sufficient.  Assume 20 user features at 8 bytes each for 100,000 users: 16 MB raw numeric values. Forty thousand products with 30 eight-byte features require 9.6 MB raw. Keys, missing-value indicators, timestamps, versions, replicas, serialization, and indexes add overhead. Fetching 200 candidate vectors separately would produce 46,400 remote lookups/second at peak. Batch reads and compact cached item features reduce remote call count; monitor payload size as well as calls.  Set a proposed 99th-percentile response target of 150 milliseconds. A sequential budget might allocate 10 ms gateway/network overhead, 20 ms candidate retrieval, 25 ms feature retrieval, 40 ms inference, 15 ms eligibility filtering and response, plus 40 ms reserve. These sum to 150 ms but do not prove the system's 99th percentile: component tails correlate, network conditions vary, and end-to-end load tests are required. Assume user interaction features should be less than five minutes old, catalog availability less than one minute old, and recommendations may fall back safely if these goals are missed. 
 Interfaces, contract, and flow   GET /recommendations?context=home&limit=20
→ {items, request_id, model_version, fallback_reason?}
feature definition: {name, type, entity_key, transformation_version,
                     event_time_semantics, freshness_limit, default}
online row: (entity_id, feature_set_version)
  → {values, source_event_time, computed_at, expires_at}
model manifest: {model_version, required_feature_set,
                 schema_hash, artifact_digest, rollout_policy}
exposure event: {request_id, model_version, candidate_ids,
                 displayed_ids, experiment_assignment, occurred_at}   A model manifest declares the required inputs; deployments must reject incompatible feature versions. Do not expose unnecessary user features in the client response. An exposure event records what the user actually saw, so offline evaluation can distinguish unseen candidates from displayed results. Restrict access to feature data and bound retention independently for raw events, derived features, and experiment logs.  [Interaction events] --> [Versioned transformations]
                             |                  |
                             v                  v
                    [Historical feature store] [Online feature store]
                             |                  ^
                    point-in-time training      | materialization
                             v                  |
                      [Model validation] --> [Versioned registry]
                                                  |
[Request] --> [Candidate retrieval] --> [Batch feature lookup]
                                                  |
                                                  v
                                          [Model inference]
                                                  |
                               [Current eligibility filter]
                                                  |
                             [Ranked response / popular fallback] 
 Progressive design: earn the model  Start with a nonpersonalized baseline: available popular items by neighborhood and category, with explicit merchant and safety rules. It establishes an availability fallback and a measurable comparison. Add offline-trained ranking only when the product question and evaluation data justify it. Keep catalog eligibility authoritative outside the model: a high predicted score never authorizes sale of unavailable stock, bypasses access rules, or overrides a merchant's removal.  Generate candidates using simple category and popularity indexes first. Fetch user features once and item features in a batch; cache shared item vectors with versioned keys. Score the candidate batch within a bounded deadline and filter current eligibility before responding. If fewer than 20 remain, fill from the safe baseline or return fewer, according to the user experience contract. Avoid unlimited retries that exceed the request's deadline.  Feature freshness requires two timestamps.  source_event_time  indicates the newest source fact incorporated;  computed_at  indicates processing time. Recomputing from yesterday's input now produces a recent computation timestamp with stale information. Check the appropriate freshness measure per feature. A missing feature and a measured zero are different values: include a missing indicator or a documented training-consistent default, and record how frequently defaults are used. 
 Training consistency and temporal leakage  Training-serving skew means training and online inference compute inputs differently. A seven-day count calculated in UTC during training and local days online is one example. Share versioned transformation logic where practical, test with fixed event sequences, and compare sampled online feature values with offline recomputation. A shared codebase alone does not guarantee identical data arrival, window boundaries, or missing-value behavior.  Point-in-time correctness means constructing each training row only from information available at that row's prediction time, subject to the system's actual availability contract. If a shopper was scored at 10:00, a purchase at 10:05 must not enter that score's features. Late-arriving historical data can also leak knowledge if a backfill uses facts not available online at 10:00. Keep event time and availability time where the use case needs both. Join features as of the example timestamp and preserve labels separately.  Use time-based evaluation splits when predicting future behavior, avoid users or sessions accidentally leaking between incompatible splits, and compare against the baseline. Offline ranking metrics are proxies; run a controlled experiment with stable assignment and latency/error guardrails before broad release. Statistical methodology belongs in a dedicated experiment lesson, but the architecture must capture assignment, exposure, outcome, and model version so analysis is possible. 
 Failures and rollout  If the online store fails, use bounded cached features only within their declared freshness window or fall back to popular eligible items. If inference exceeds its deadline, return fallback and count the timeout. Do not silently serve arbitrary default vectors for every user and call the resulting output personalized. Track fallback rate, feature age, missing-feature rate, schema rejection, batch size, inference latency, and output score distributions.  Deploy a model and its compatible feature set together through a manifest. Preload artifacts, validate checksum and schema, warm instances, and route a small fraction of traffic before expansion. Shadow mode computes predictions without changing the displayed result; it helps measure latency and output differences but does not measure actual user response to the shadow output. Canary rollout exposes a small real audience and therefore requires business guardrails. Keep the previous compatible artifact and feature contract for rollback.  A traffic spike can overwhelm feature storage before model CPUs. Apply admission controls, cap candidates, batch reads, and degrade in a measured order. Cache keys containing only user ID can accidentally mix model or feature versions; include the relevant version and context. Limit cache lifetime for personalization, and prevent cross-user cache leakage through authenticated key construction. A feature pipeline outage should not make checkout unavailable: recommendation and purchase correctness have different dependency budgets. 
 Alternatives, evolution, and interview close  Reject a synchronous full-history warehouse query on every recommendation request: it moves large scans into a tight latency budget. Reject adding a vector database merely because the feature is called AI; ordinary indexed candidate retrieval may satisfy this compact model. Embedding retrieval becomes justified when learned similarity improves candidate quality under measured cost and latency. Reject running a large generative model for this assumed ranking workload without evidence of benefit.  At multi-region scale, replicate relatively stable item features, route user state deliberately, and document freshness during pipeline partitions. Keep model artifacts identical by digest, but allow controlled regional rollouts. Cost includes feature computation, online reads, model execution, experiment logging, retraining, and operational support. Compare benefit with the popular baseline and remove complexity that fails to earn its cost.   Practice: offline accuracy improves dramatically after a backfill, but online results do not. What do you inspect?  Check temporal leakage, availability-time joins, changed metric definitions, selection bias, feature defaults, train/serve transformations, and exposure logging. Reconstruct a historical request using only data actually available then. A larger model is not the first repair.    Follow-ups and rubric   Follow-ups:  How do deletion requests propagate? What does a safe fallback show? How do you roll back incompatible inputs?  Strong:  defines freshness and feature versions, separates eligibility from prediction, identifies leakage, and includes a baseline.  Weak:  adds a vector database without a retrieval requirement, treats recent computation as fresh data, or claims offline accuracy proves business impact.   Technical reference checked 2026-10-19:  Feast point-in-time join documentation  explains reconstructing feature state at historical timestamps. Availability-time handling, operational budgets, and model choices here are explicit exercise design decisions.  A short spoken walkthrough   Candidate:  May recommendations fall back when features are too old?  Interviewer:  Yes, use a safe non-personalized list.  Candidate:  I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.  Interviewer:  Your latency is excellent but the model quality falls. What do you change first?  Candidate:  I inspect feature age, missingness, model/schema version and training-serving agreement. Adding replicas does not repair wrong inputs. I canary the model and transformation together with quality and latency guardrails, then roll back the versioned bundle if they regress. Eligibility remains an authoritative filter, independent of model scores.  This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Case 11 · Book a community pickup appointment
text:
Corner Market partners with community clinics to schedule equipment pickups and service appointments. An available calendar cell is a hint; a confirmed booking is a promise enforced by a transaction. 
 Exact interview prompt  Design appointment booking across 2,000 community clinics. Users browse available slots, book one, cancel, and retry after network failures. Prevent double booking and explain how your design evolves. 
 Clarification dialogue and requirements   Interviewer:  “Can users choose arbitrary durations?”  Candidate:  “May I begin with fixed, pre-generated, single-capacity slots? Overlapping variable-duration appointments require interval conflict detection.”  Interviewer:  “Yes. Confirmations must never overlap for a slot.”  Candidate:  “Then the booking transaction, not the cached calendar, owns that invariant.” 
 Assume each clinic offers 100 slots/day, published 90 days ahead. One account can book multiple distinct slots, subject to abuse limits. Cancellation releases capacity; no payment or temporary holds in the first version. Ask about rescheduling: support an atomic move within the same database. Store instants in UTC with the clinic's named time zone for display and schedule generation. A local time can be ambiguous or nonexistent around daylight-saving changes; generate slots using an explicit policy and preserve the resulting instant. The examples are fictional assumptions. 
 Propose 99.9% monthly booking availability and p95 server response below 300 ms under normal regional operation. Successful confirmation means a durable transaction committed. Availability browsing may lag by five seconds; booking always checks current authoritative state. Users receive a conflict response when another person wins. Notifications are asynchronous and do not determine whether the appointment exists. 
 Work the numbers  2,000 clinics × 100 slots/day × 90 days = 18 million slot rows. At 200 logical bytes/row, that is 3.6 GB before indexes, row overhead, booking history, replicas, and backups. Three full copies of those logical bytes alone total 10.8 GB. Assume 200 peak mutations/s and a measured or hypothesized 50 ms mean database residence time. Little's law gives average in-flight database work L = arrival rate × residence time = 200/s × 0.05 s = 10 concurrent operations. This is not a recommendation for a ten-connection pool: transaction contention, headroom, failover, and tail latency still require measurement. 
 Assume 20 browse requests per mutation: 4,000 peak browse requests/s. Cache clinic-day availability for up to five seconds, coalesce concurrent misses, and bound fallback concurrency. A single famous clinic can still create a hot slot even when aggregate database load is small; its successful write capacity is one booking, regardless of infrastructure size. 
 API, schema, and exact enforcement   GET /v1/clinics/{id}/slots?date=2026-11-03
POST /v1/bookings
Idempotency-Key: client-request-uuid
{ slot_id: "s42" }
→ 201 { booking_id, slot_id, state: "confirmed" }
DELETE /v1/bookings/{id} → 204
POST /v1/bookings/{id}/reschedule { new_slot_id }

slots(id PRIMARY KEY, clinic_id, starts_at, ends_at,
      active_booking_id NULL, version,
      UNIQUE(clinic_id, starts_at), CHECK(ends_at > starts_at))
bookings(id PRIMARY KEY, slot_id, user_id, state, created_at)
requests(user_id, key, request_hash, response,
         UNIQUE(user_id, key))
outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, booking_id, event_type)  
 Enforce one active occupant with an atomic conditional update:  UPDATE slots SET active_booking_id=:booking WHERE id=:slot AND active_booking_id IS NULL . Require exactly one affected row, then insert booking, request response, and notification outbox row in the same transaction. Roll back all work on failure. The slot primary key makes all competing updates contend on the same authoritative row. An idempotency key identifies one intended action across retries; a repeated key with different input is rejected. Serialize concurrent uses of the same key using its unique request record inside the transaction. 
 Labeled architecture and progression  BROWSE: client → calendar API → clinic-day cache → slot database
BOOK:   client → authenticated booking API → database transaction
                                  [slot + booking + request + outbox]
                                                          ↓ dispatcher
                                                 notification worker
INVALIDATE: committed change → cache invalidation (TTL is fallback) 
 Start with a relational database, stateless API, and no cache until browsing warrants it. Cancellation locks the booking and clears the slot only when active_booking_id matches that booking, then updates state and writes an outbox event in one transaction. This comparison prevents a delayed duplicate cancellation from clearing a later occupant's booking. Repeated cancellation returns the existing cancelled outcome. 
 Rescheduling first locks and re-reads the booking row and verifies it remains confirmed and owned by the caller, using the same booking-then-slot lock order as cancellation. It then locks old and new slot rows in a consistent ID order to reduce deadlocks, verifies the old slot still points to this booking and the new slot is available, releases old capacity, claims new capacity, and updates the booking atomically. On conflict, preserve the old appointment. Retry deadlock victims with the same idempotency key and bounded backoff. A transaction boundary matters more here than introducing a queue. 
 Three failure traces    Two users book s42:  A updates the empty slot and commits. B waits on the row, then its conditional predicate no longer matches. B changes zero rows and receives 409. A stale browse cache cannot override this result.   Commit succeeds; response disappears:  the client retries the same key. The stored response returns the original booking. A new key would mean a new intended operation and must not be substituted automatically.   Notification worker crashes after sending:  outbox replay may send a duplicate notification. The booking remains confirmed once. Include a stable event ID and use provider deduplication when supported; otherwise notifications remain at least once.  
 Challenge, alternatives, and operations   Interviewer:  “Why not lock the slot in Redis?”  Candidate:  “A cache lock expiring during a slow database operation can permit two holders. The database conditional update already enforces the invariant where durable state lives. I would use a distributed lock only with a demonstrated need and a fencing mechanism enforced by the resource.” A fencing mechanism rejects stale owners using increasing ownership versions. 
 Reject read-then-write availability checks without atomic enforcement. Reject serializing every clinic through one global queue because independent slots need no shared order. If variable durations arrive, fixed slot uniqueness is insufficient: use interval reservations with an exclusion constraint or serialize each resource's overlap check and insertion under an appropriate transaction policy. Do not assume a row-level check constraint can enforce arbitrary cross-row non-overlap. 
 Monitor booking latency, conflict rate, lock wait time, deadlocks, request-key conflicts, outbox lag, and cache age. A high conflict rate may reflect real scarcity rather than a broken service. Protect popular releases with admission control and per-account limits. Audit staff overrides and cancellation ownership. Restore drills must verify slot pointers and booking state together. 
 Evolve temporary holds only with an explicit expiry authority: a hold consumes capacity until a database-checked deadline; a late confirmation must atomically verify that hold still owns the slot. Partition by clinic when measured pressure warrants it. Cross-partition rescheduling then requires a different product contract or coordination; explain that added complexity before promising the original atomic behavior. 
 Follow-ups and rubric   Practice: cancellation retries after another user has booked the released slot. What prevents damage?  Clear only if the slot still points to the cancelled booking. The old request must not unconditionally clear active_booking_id.    Practice: does five-second calendar caching allow five seconds of double booking?  No. Caching affects displayed availability only. Every confirmation uses the authoritative conditional transaction.    Strong:  identifies the slot invariant, names the atomic enforcement, handles ambiguous responses, and preserves the old booking on failed reschedule.  Weak:  equates a cached “available” flag with a reservation or proposes locks without expiry/failure semantics. Principal depth includes interval evolution and cross-partition contract changes. 
 Checked 2026-10-19:  PostgreSQL constraints  and  explicit locking . Numbers and service objectives are worked assumptions.

title: Case 12 · Defend inventory across regions
text:
Corner Market expands internationally. Regional independence sounds attractive until two buyers reserve the final bicycle during a network partition. This capstone makes the availability, latency, and correctness contract explicit. 
 Exact interview prompt  Design multi-region inventory reservation at 20,000 peak reads/s and 2,000 peak writes/s. Prevent overselling, target zero loss of acknowledged writes and recovery within five minutes, and explain regional failure behavior. 
 Clarification dialogue and objectives   Candidate:  “Does zero loss mean any single regional failure, and can a partitioned minority reject writes?”  Interviewer:  “Yes. Single-region failure is the fault model. No overselling; reads may be stale.”  Candidate:  “I will require durable cross-region quorum before acknowledging a write. I cannot also promise every isolated region accepts writes.” 
 Recovery point objective (RPO) is the allowed loss of acknowledged data; assume RPO 0 for a single-region failure under the stated durable quorum model. Recovery time objective (RTO) is the time to restore the specified service; target under five minutes, demonstrated through exercises. These objectives do not cover destruction of every copy, operator corruption without recoverable history, or arbitrary simultaneous regional failures. Define the fault model before claiming a guarantee. 
 Assume 99.95% monthly time-based write availability. Over a 30-day month, the error budget is 30 × 24 × 60 × 0.0005 = 21.6 minutes. A four-minute incident would consume about 18.5% of that budget. This is a time-based simplification; a request-based service-level indicator measures failed eligible requests instead. Reads target p95 under 100 ms from local derived views, with explicit freshness. Writes have a separate latency budget. 
 Latency and capacity reasoning  Assume hypothetical 80 ms inter-region round-trip time (RTT), meaning a request and response across regions take 80 ms before durable storage and processing. A coordinated write requiring that exchange cannot achieve a 50 ms response under those assumptions. Negotiate a feasible write objective, for example p95 under 250 ms subject to measurements. Parallel local processing does not remove the communication lower bound. Actual topology and consensus protocol determine the precise path. 
 At 2,000 writes/s and assumed 250 ms average in-flight duration, Little's law predicts 500 concurrent requests. This uses an assumed mean, not the p95 target as measured evidence. At 1 KB logical mutation payload, peak application writes are 2 MB/s before protocol, replication, indexes, and log overhead. Reads at 20,000/s with an assumed 90% cache hit rate leave 2,000/s view-store reads; cold-cache tests must cover far more. The final-item hotspot is a serial correctness problem, even when bandwidth is ample. 
 API, schema, and invariant   POST /v1/reservations
Idempotency-Key: buyer-request-uuid
{ sku, quantity: 1, ttl_seconds: 300 }
→ 201 { reservation_id, state: "held", expires_at, version }
POST /v1/reservations/{id}/confirm → confirmed | expired
DELETE /v1/reservations/{id} → released
GET /v1/items/{sku}/availability → { approximate_available, as_of }

inventory(sku PRIMARY KEY, available CHECK(available >= 0), version)
reservations(id PRIMARY KEY, sku, quantity, state, expires_at,
             buyer_id, version)
requests(buyer_id, key, request_hash, response, UNIQUE(buyer_id,key))
outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, reservation_id, version, type)  
 The invariant is available ≥ 0, with each held or confirmed unit accounted for exactly once. Under the authoritative transactional database, execute  UPDATE inventory SET available=available-:q, version=version+1 WHERE sku=:sku AND available>=:q , require one affected row, then insert reservation, request response, and event in the same transaction. A check constraint is defense in depth; the conditional update decides acceptance. The database's selected transaction and consensus implementation must preserve this atomicity across failover. 
 Labeled architecture and progression  Region A clients → router ─┐
Region B clients → router ─┼→ current partition leader / authority
Region C clients → router ─┘          ↓ ordered transaction log
                            A replica ↔ B replica ↔ C replica
                            majority durable commit → acknowledge
                                     ↓ change events
                              regional read views/cache
CONTROL: consensus election + term/epoch → stale leader fenced 
 Begin with one authoritative write region and local replicas, then identify the unmet disaster objective: local-only durability does not provide RPO 0 for regional loss. Select a proven database offering the required cross-region synchronous durability and transactional behavior, and verify its documented failure modes. Do not implement consensus in application code. With three voting replicas placed in three independent regions, a majority can survive loss of one region if the remaining two communicate; placement, durable acknowledgment, and election configuration must be validated. 
 Partition inventory by sku so independent products scale. Each partition has one current logical authority. Consensus terms or epochs distinguish leadership generations; replicas reject operations from stale leaders. Application routing follows the elected authority and never promotes a disconnected copy simply because it is reachable. Consensus coordinates ordered state across replicas; replication alone does not imply safe ownership changes. 
 Three failure traces    Region A loses connectivity:  if B and C form a majority, they elect an authorized leader and resume writes after election. A cannot commit alone and rejects or times out writes. Local stale reads may continue only under the approved display contract. Checkout routes to the majority.   Commit acknowledgment is lost:  the buyer retries the original request key. The durable request record returns the same reservation. Do not decrement inventory again. If outcome cannot yet be established, report pending/retryable status rather than claiming failure and issuing a new operation.   Hold expiry races confirmation:  both transactions condition on current held state and database-evaluated expiry. Exactly one transition wins. Expiry restores quantity only if it changes held to expired; confirmation succeeds only before the deadline and changes held to confirmed. Duplicate expiry cannot increment stock twice.  
 Challenge and defended choice   Interviewer:  “I need 50 ms writes everywhere, even during disconnection.”  Candidate:  “That conflicts with the 80 ms coordination path and our single shared-stock contract. We can change the contract by allocating regional quotas. A region sells only its locally owned quota, and transferring quota requires coordination. That buys local acceptance while some regions may show sold out despite remote stock.” This is escrow allocation: distribute bounded rights whose total never exceeds global inventory. 
 Reject unconstrained active-active counters merged after the fact: two regions may each sell the final unit, and conflict resolution cannot undo a physical promise. Reject asynchronous failover when claiming RPO 0; acknowledged data may not have reached the promoted region. Escrow is a legitimate alternative when quota fragmentation is acceptable, not a universal substitute for transactions. Allocation preserves the stock-rights bound, but does not independently provide RPO 0: reservations accepted only inside an isolated region can disappear if that region is then lost. Zero-loss acknowledgment still needs durable copies outside the regional failure domain, adding coordination latency or forcing rejection during isolation. If local-only isolated acceptance is required, explicitly renegotiate the durability/RPO contract rather than retaining the original promise. 
 Operations and evolution  Monitor quorum health, leader changes, replication/commit latency, rejected minority writes, reservation conflict rate, hold-expiry lag, and read-view age. Alert on user-visible symptoms and budget burn, not every election. Run regional isolation and recovery exercises, measure routing and retry convergence, and verify acknowledged reservations after failover. RTO includes detection, election, routing, and safe client recovery, not merely starting a replacement process. 
 Keep backups and point-in-time recovery for accidental deletion; quorum replicates mistakes too. Roll out schema changes compatibly across versions. Reconcile inventory movements with durable reservation events and investigate invariant violations rather than silently resetting counts. Add regional quota allocation only for appropriate product classes; high-demand scarce items may retain coordinated writes. Measure the cost of extra copies, cross-region traffic, and write latency against the business value of the stated disaster objective. 
 Follow-ups and rubric   Practice: the read cache says one item remains, but reservation fails. Is the design broken?  No. The displayed number is approximate. The authoritative conditional transaction decides, returns a clear conflict, and prompts a refresh. Misrepresenting the display as guaranteed would be a product contract error.    Practice: why does three replicas not automatically prove RPO 0?  All copies might share a failure domain, acknowledgment might precede durable replication, or failover might promote an incomplete replica. Verify placement, commit rules, failure scope, and safe promotion semantics.    Strong:  states the partition behavior, enforces stock atomically, computes the latency lower bound and budget, and distinguishes recovery objectives from evidence.  Weak:  promises low latency, universal availability, and strict shared-stock correctness simultaneously. Principal depth includes quota alternatives, rollout compatibility, and tested recovery ownership. 
 Checked 2026-10-19:  PostgreSQL constraints ;  Raft consensus paper . This architecture specifies required guarantees rather than asserting a particular vendor deployment meets them.

title: Practice · failure probes and self-assessment
text: Use a 45-minute timer for a full case, or five minutes for one failure probe below. Write your answer before opening the sample. These are original exercises; sample answers show a defensible direction rather than a universal architecture.  Probe 1: A response is lost after an order commits. Show a safe retry protocol.   Reveal sample reasoning  Persist a client-scoped idempotency key, request fingerprint and outcome in the same transaction as the order. Retry the same key. Reject changed payloads. Return the stored outcome; expire keys only after defining the retry window. A volatile cache alone cannot protect a durable side effect.   Probe 2: Two requests each observe one remaining item. Both purchase it. Identify the broken invariant and repair it.   Reveal sample reasoning  The invariant is reserved quantity plus sold quantity never exceeding stock. A read followed by an unconditional update permits both reads before either write. Use a conditional atomic decrement and check affected rows inside the reservation transaction. Add a unique request key. A Python mutex in one replica does not protect another replica.   Probe 3: A cache says a user may see a private photo. Permission has just been revoked. What happens?   Reveal sample reasoning  Revocation is a security boundary. Do not authorize from a potentially stale content cache. Re-check authoritative permission or a versioned policy with an explicitly bounded revocation contract; invalidate delivery credentials and caches as needed. A short expiry reduces exposure but does not meet immediate revocation.   Probe 4: At 1,000 requests/s with 200 ms mean time in system, how many requests are in flight?   Reveal sample reasoning  At stable load Little’s law gives L = λW = 1,000/s × 0.2 s = 200. This uses averages at the same boundary, not p99 latency. It does not imply 200 CPU cores. Queueing, downstream connections and asynchronous waits matter.   Probe 5: A worker completes an email then crashes before acknowledging. Can the queue guarantee no duplicate email?   Reveal sample reasoning  Redelivery can repeat the email. A queue cannot make its acknowledgment atomic with an arbitrary mail provider. Use a provider-supported stable deduplication key, or accept possible duplicates with a durable attempt ledger and reconciliation. A local done flag written after sending retains the crash window.   Probe 6: A five-node consensus group loses three nodes. May two survivors accept writes?   Reveal sample reasoning  A majority is three. Two cannot safely elect a leader and commit new entries under the assumed Raft model. Serve only reads whose semantics are justified; a stale read must be labeled as such. Restoring availability by forming a new cluster without a recovery protocol risks losing acknowledged state.   Probe 7: A seller with ten million followers posts. Your feed uses write fanout. What changes?   Reveal sample reasoning  Ordinary-seller assumptions no longer bound fanout cost. Use a hybrid: precompute ordinary feeds and merge high-fanout sellers at read time. Preserve a durable post log, deduplicate by post ID, cap work per request and define freshness under backlog. The threshold comes from measurements, not an arbitrary celebrity number.   Probe 8: A search index still contains a deleted listing. How do you meet a five-second deletion requirement?   Reveal sample reasoning  Index removals through a durable versioned event, measure propagation lag, and filter against a deletion tombstone or current visibility check at serving time. Replay must not resurrect older versions. A periodic full rebuild alone cannot bound deletion latency.   Probe 9: A schedule fires twice after a lease timeout. Explain fencing.   Reveal sample reasoning  A fencing token is a monotonically increasing ownership epoch. Each mutation to the protected resource includes it; the resource rejects older epochs. Lease expiry alone cannot stop a paused worker from waking up. External effects still need their own idempotency or fencing support.   Probe 10: An active-active inventory design merges counters after a network partition. Is overselling prevented?   Reveal sample reasoning  No: both regions can spend the same remaining unit. Route ownership to one region, use coordination and reject unavailable writes, or allocate non-overlapping bounded stock rights to each region. Reconciliation detects an oversell after the fact; it does not preserve the invariant.   Probe 11: A streaming count changes after late events. Is the old answer wrong?   Reveal sample reasoning  Define event time, allowed lateness and whether results are provisional. Emit revisions or an explicit finalization boundary. Deduplicate stable event IDs for the agreed retention window. Keep source records for replay and reconcile against batch totals. Different windows and correction rules can both be valid if the contract is explicit.   Probe 12: Feature serving is fast, but recommendations degrade after deployment. Where do you investigate?   Reveal sample reasoning  Check feature version, freshness, missingness and training-serving transformation agreement before adding hardware. Pin model and feature schema versions, compare offline and online values, and canary with quality and operational guardrails. Safe fallback may be a non-personalized ranking; low latency alone does not imply correct predictions.   A reusable scoring sheet  Score each dimension 0 (missing), 1 (named), 2 (defended with a concrete trace), or 3 (survives a changed assumption): scope; units and capacity; API/data contract; correctness; failures/recovery; operations/security; alternatives/cost; communication. This is a learning rubric, not an employer hiring rubric. A total can hide a dangerous correctness gap: repeat any case whose invariant or acknowledgment boundary scores below 2.  For principal practice add evidence for migration ownership, organizational interfaces, failure containment, measurable decision triggers and reversal cost. Ask a partner to change one requirement halfway through. Record whether you adapt using evidence or merely add components.  Interview-platform interpretation  Sources reviewed 19 October 2026. These observations inform practice structure; they do not establish question frequency or any employer’s hidden scoring.    Source and evidence type  Interpretation used in this course     LeetCode Discuss: droplet1’s framework  · community account, not official LeetCode hiring guidance  The author emphasizes explaining assumptions and decision logic. We turn that into a trace and a rejected alternative per case. Personal offer claims are anecdotal and are not evidence of effectiveness.     Hello Interview: Delivery Framework  · interview-preparation platform’s own advice  It recommends reaching a working design before deep dives and using estimates when they affect decisions. We require an end-to-end request path and tie arithmetic to a bottleneck. The course’s prompts and worked solutions are original.     Amazon SDE III preparation  · official employer guidance for that role  Use it to confirm the stated process and preparation areas for that employer and role. Our principal rubric is a teaching device and is not represented as Amazon’s hiring standard.    The case families—read-heavy lookup, fanout, persistent connections, large objects, retrieval, admission control, leased work, transactional state, event aggregation and model serving—exercise different constraints. Their inclusion is a curriculum choice, not a ranking of commonly asked questions. No paid material was accessed or reproduced.

title: Glossary · precise definitions and practical meaning
text: Each entry gives an original precise definition, a plain-English meaning, a relatable analogy with its limit, and a concrete system example. Analogies aid intuition; the definition and explicit contract govern correctness. References support the stated technical concept, not the invented market examples. Sources checked 2026-10-19.   Invariant   Precise definition:  A predicate over system state that is true initially and preserved by every permitted state transition.   Plain English:  A rule the system must never break, including during competing requests and recovery.   Analogy and its limit:  A shop cannot hand out more numbered collection tickets than it has allocated goods; unlike a physical counter, software copies can disagree.   Concrete example:  If stock begins at five, accepting two reservations of three violates the nonnegative-stock invariant. Protect the decrement where authoritative state changes.   Herlihy and Wing: correctness and invariants  · checked 2026-10-19.    Atomicity   Precise definition:  A transaction property under which its participating state changes commit as one unit or have no committed effect.   Plain English:  Either all the included database work counts, or none does.   Analogy and its limit:  A sealed parcel contains every promised item or is not dispatched; the analogy does not make a separate courier transaction atomic.   Concrete example:  Creating a reservation and decrementing inventory belong in one database transaction. A payment-provider call outside that database is not automatically rolled back with it.   PostgreSQL: transactions  · checked 2026-10-19.    Isolation   Precise definition:  The transaction property specifying permitted observations and interference among concurrently executing transactions.   Plain English:  It controls how overlapping database operations may affect one another.   Analogy and its limit:  Separate checkout desks can share inventory under different coordination rules; physical desk separation alone does not prevent selling the same last item.   Concrete example:  Two transactions reading the same stock then writing independently can lose a decrement. Choose an atomic update or appropriate locking and isolation; merely writing BEGIN does not establish every desired guarantee.   PostgreSQL: isolation levels  · checked 2026-10-19.    Linearizability   Precise definition:  A concurrent-object correctness condition in which operations admit a legal sequential ordering, with each taking effect between invocation and response and respecting real-time precedence.   Plain English:  Once a write finishes, a later read cannot behave as if that write has not happened.   Analogy and its limit:  One authoritative ticket clerk assigns a single order to purchases; distributed implementations need not literally use one clerk.   Concrete example:  After a stock update completes, a subsequent linearizable read observes it or a later valid update, rather than an old replica value.   Herlihy and Wing: linearizability  · checked 2026-10-19.    Serializability   Precise definition:  An isolation guarantee that committed concurrent transactions are equivalent to some serial execution of those transactions.   Plain English:  Overlapping transactions produce a result possible if complete transactions ran one at a time.   Analogy and its limit:  A manager can arrange whole order slips into an equivalent processing sequence; this does not require matching wall-clock completion order.   Concrete example:  A multi-row inventory rule remains correct if every serial transaction preserves it. Serializable databases may abort conflicting attempts, so applications must retry the whole transaction safely.   PostgreSQL: serializable isolation  · checked 2026-10-19.    Idempotency   Precise definition:  The property that repeating an operation has the same intended effect on server state as applying it once, under the operation’s defined identity and scope.   Plain English:  A retry should not multiply the business action.   Analogy and its limit:  Presenting the same numbered collection ticket again does not earn another parcel; a new ticket represents a different request.   Concrete example:  Repeated checkout requests reuse one shopper-scoped key and unchanged body. The service stores the result and rejects incompatible key reuse. Identical response bytes are not required, and protection needs a documented retention window.   RFC 9110 §9.2.2  · checked 2026-10-19.    Ambiguous outcome   Precise definition:  A caller knowledge state in which available observations do not determine whether an operation committed or produced its external effect.   Plain English:  No answer does not mean no action happened.   Analogy and its limit:  A shopkeeper cannot hear whether a shouted collection request was fulfilled; shouting again may duplicate it. Unlike the analogy, software can preserve a durable request identity.   Concrete example:  A provider captures payment but its response is lost. Keep the attempt pending, query or safely retry using its original identity, and reconcile before asserting failure.   RFC 9110: retries and method semantics  · checked 2026-10-19.    Consensus   Precise definition:  A distributed agreement problem requiring participating nodes to decide consistently on values despite a specified failure model, with progress under stated communication and availability assumptions.   Plain English:  Nodes agree which decision counts, even when some stop responding.   Analogy and its limit:  A committee records one approved motion; software protocols must also handle delayed messages and changing leadership, not human judgment.   Concrete example:  A five-voter Raft group uses a majority of three. Three connected functioning voters can make progress under suitable timing assumptions; arbitrary malicious behavior lies outside Raft’s crash-failure model.   Raft: agreement and leader election  · checked 2026-10-19.    Quorum   Precise definition:  A subset of participants sufficient for a protocol step, chosen so required subsets intersect in ways the protocol’s safety argument needs.   Plain English:  Enough relevant members must respond before an action counts.   Analogy and its limit:  A committee may require three of five signatures; signatures alone do not specify how contradictory proposals are handled.   Concrete example:  Two majorities of a five-node set overlap. That overlap helps consensus safety, but R + W greater than N alone does not prove linearizability without version, ordering, failure, and repair rules.   Raft: majority quorums  · checked 2026-10-19.    Replication   Precise definition:  Maintaining multiple copies of a dataset or state machine through a mechanism that propagates updates among copies.   Plain English:  Keep other copies so one failure need not remove all usable data.   Analogy and its limit:  Several shop ledgers copy each day’s changes; copying yesterday’s mistake reproduces the mistake rather than creating a backup.   Concrete example:  A leader accepts a reservation while an asynchronous replica has not yet applied it. Reading that replica may show old stock. The acknowledgment and failover policy determine which acknowledged writes can survive a failure.   PostgreSQL: high availability and replication  · checked 2026-10-19.    Partitioning / sharding   Precise definition:  Partitioning divides a dataset into disjoint subsets; sharding typically assigns subsets to independently managed database nodes using a placement rule.   Plain English:  Different owners hold different pieces of the data.   Analogy and its limit:  Separate market stalls own different shelves; copying every shelf to another building would instead be replication. The analogy does not address cross-stall transactions.   Concrete example:  Store identifier routes inventory to a shard. Shopper history may need a separate derived index. One popular item can still overload its owner. A network partition means broken communication, not this deliberate division.   PostgreSQL: table partitioning; cross-node sharding distinction is course terminology  · checked 2026-10-19.    Backpressure   Precise definition:  A flow-control mechanism by which downstream capacity constrains upstream production or admission of work.   Plain English:  Slow down incoming work when the next stage cannot keep up.   Analogy and its limit:  A cashier stops accepting baskets when the packing bench is full; a warehouse-sized waiting line only delays overload. Unlike people, software producers need explicit signals or enforced limits.   Concrete example:  A bounded queue makes producers wait or reject work at capacity. If 250 jobs arrive per second and workers finish 150, backlog otherwise grows by 100 each second.   Java Flow: demand-based flow control  · checked 2026-10-19.    Outbox   Precise definition:  A durable event record committed atomically with business state and later published by an independent relay.   Plain English:  Save the notification obligation with the change, then deliver it afterward.   Analogy and its limit:  A shop staples a dispatch slip to the completed order record; a runner may copy a slip twice, so recipients still need duplicate handling.   Concrete example:  An order and OrderConfirmed event commit in one transaction. A relay publishes the event and crashes before recording progress. It publishes again after restart; consumers deduplicate by stable event identifier.   AWS: transactional outbox  · checked 2026-10-19.    Fencing token   Precise definition:  A monotonically ordered ownership generation carried with operations and enforced by the protected resource to reject superseded owners.   Plain English:  The storage system refuses commands from yesterday’s owner.   Analogy and its limit:  A new supervisor receives a higher-numbered authorization badge; this works only if the warehouse checks the badge on every protected action.   Concrete example:  Worker A pauses holding token seven. Worker B obtains token eight and writes. When A resumes, storage rejects token seven. Generating tokens without atomically enforcing them at the resource does not prevent stale writes.   Chubby: sequencers and stale lock holders  · checked 2026-10-19.    Lease   Precise definition:  A time-bounded grant of rights whose continued validity depends on a defined expiration and renewal protocol.   Plain English:  You own permission for a limited time unless it is renewed.   Analogy and its limit:  A market stall rental expires at closing time; the old tenant may still physically remain there. Software pauses likewise do not stop when permission expires.   Concrete example:  A worker’s lease expires during a long pause. Another worker becomes owner, but the first can resume executing. Use resource-enforced fencing when stale execution could corrupt shared state, and state clock and timing assumptions.   Chubby: leases and sessions  · checked 2026-10-19.    Watermark   Precise definition:  A stream-processing progress indication describing how far event time is considered advanced under the system’s timestamp and lateness policy.   Plain English:  The processor estimates which earlier time windows are ready to evaluate.   Analogy and its limit:  A delivery clerk announces that the morning mail is probably complete; a delayed envelope can still arrive, depending on the policy. It is not a universal proof of completeness.   Concrete example:  A five-minute order-count window closes when its watermark passes the boundary. A late offline order may trigger a correction, be retained separately, or be dropped according to the documented rule.   Flink: event time and watermarks  · checked 2026-10-19.    SLI / SLO   Precise definition:  A service level indicator quantifies a service behavior; a service level objective specifies a target for that indicator over a defined population and time window.   Plain English:  Measure what users experience, then state how good it should be.   Analogy and its limit:  A grocer measures the fraction of collections ready on time and sets a target; unlike a vague promise, the measurement needs eligibility and timing rules.   Concrete example:  Count eligible catalog requests returning a correct result within 300 milliseconds, targeting 99.9 percent over thirty days. A process health check measures something narrower.   Google SRE: indicators and objectives  · checked 2026-10-19.    RPO / RTO   Precise definition:  Recovery point objective specifies targeted maximum data loss measured backward in time; recovery time objective specifies targeted maximum time to restore the defined service after disruption.   Plain English:  How much recent work may be lost, and how long recovery may take.   Analogy and its limit:  A shop can reconstruct sales only to its last copied ledger and needs time to reopen; software recovery also includes routing, credentials, and validation.   Concrete example:  A five-minute RPO and thirty-minute RTO require a tested procedure that restores sufficiently recent data and usable service inside those targets. Objectives are not demonstrated achievements.   AWS Well-Architected: disaster recovery objectives  · checked 2026-10-19.    p99 latency   Precise definition:  The ninety-ninth percentile of measured operation durations for a specified population, observation boundary, interval, and percentile calculation convention.   Plain English:  Approximately ninety-nine percent of measured operations finish at or below that duration.   Analogy and its limit:  In a sorted line of one hundred collection times, look near the slow end rather than the average; real percentile estimators need not select exactly one sample.   Concrete example:  A 300-millisecond server p99 excludes client-side connection failures unless measured there. Adding three dependencies’ p99 values does not give the request p99 because their slow observations may differ.   Google SRE: latency distributions and measurement  · checked 2026-10-19.    CDN   Precise definition:  A content delivery network distributes content-serving infrastructure across network locations, commonly caching origin responses nearer consumers.   Plain English:  Serve reusable bytes from a nearby copy instead of the main application each time.   Analogy and its limit:  Neighborhood collection lockers save everyone a trip to the central shop; a locker does not decide whether a customer is entitled to a private parcel.   Concrete example:  A product image with a versioned public URL can be cached at edge locations. Private order receipts need deliberate authorization and cache policy. Proximity can improve delivery without guaranteeing the newest origin state.   RFC 9111: shared-cache behavior; CDN example is illustrative  · checked 2026-10-19.    TTL   Precise definition:  Time to live is a configured validity or retention duration whose exact start point and expiration behavior depend on the protocol or storage system.   Plain English:  An entry has a time limit, under specific rules.   Analogy and its limit:  A price label marked valid for sixty seconds expires, but replacing it with an already old label does not make the price current.   Concrete example:  A cache entry written from a lagging replica can expire sixty seconds after insertion yet describe an older fact. State whether expiration triggers deletion, revalidation, or refusal; TTL alone does not eliminate stale-fill races.   RFC 9111: freshness lifetime and age  · checked 2026-10-19.    Fanout   Precise definition:  Expansion of one input operation or event into multiple downstream deliveries, requests, or materialized updates.   Plain English:  One thing happening creates work for many destinations.   Analogy and its limit:  A grocer sends one sale announcement to every subscriber; the analogy hides failures and duplicate deliveries that software must handle explicitly.   Concrete example:  A post with ten thousand followers may create ten thousand inbox updates with fanout-on-write, or be combined into feeds during reads. Large follower skew changes the cost. Define whether partial delivery, retries, ordering, and duplicate recipients are acceptable.   RabbitMQ: fanout exchange publish/subscribe example  · checked 2026-10-19.    Cursor pagination   Precise definition:  A pagination method that resumes traversal from an encoded position in a defined ordering, often using the last observed ordering key.   Plain English:  Continue after where you stopped instead of skipping a count of rows.   Analogy and its limit:  A bookmark identifies the last shelf position visited; rearranging shelves can still change the next page. The bookmark alone does not freeze the catalog.   Concrete example:  Order history sorts by created_at and unique order_id, returning the last pair in an opaque cursor. Specify snapshot behavior and use a unique tiebreaker. Large OFFSET queries otherwise compute skipped rows.   PostgreSQL: ordering and OFFSET costs; cursor design is the course example  · checked 2026-10-19.    Observability   Precise definition:  The capacity to infer relevant internal system behavior from externally available outputs and telemetry.   Plain English:  Have enough useful evidence to explain what happened and why.   Analogy and its limit:  A grocer combines till totals, delivery notes, and queue observations to diagnose a delay; collecting more paper without a question does not improve understanding.   Concrete example:  Metrics show rising checkout failures, traces locate slow inventory calls, and correlated logs explain lock contention. Include business outcomes and careful sampling. Telemetry that leaks personal data or cannot connect request stages creates new problems rather than sufficient visibility.   OpenTelemetry: observability and telemetry signals  · checked 2026-10-19.    Training-serving skew   Precise definition:  A mismatch between the features, transformations, distributions, or data availability used during model training and those encountered when serving predictions.   Plain English:  The model is taught with a view of the world different from the one it gets in use.   Analogy and its limit:  A grocer trains assistants using tomorrow’s complete demand report, then asks them to predict today with partial information; real models can also differ through code and pipelines.   Concrete example:  Training computes a seven-day purchase count using future-complete data, while online inference uses delayed events. Use point-in-time joins, shared definitions, freshness checks, and comparison monitoring.   Google: Rules of Machine Learning, training-serving skew  · checked 2026-10-19.
